Honestly, can't we simply deprecate the UTF-7 codec and schedule its removal?

I think it is wrong. The UTF-7 codec is the part of many standards (especially in telecommunication industry), and removing it would break applications and harm Python position. It is important enough to be included in the stdlib. We could make it disabled by default, although there were no precedents, so we do not know how to handle this.

We could impose the limit for the maximal length of the Base64-encoded section, but I am not aware of the existing of such limitation in the standards, so this may break things. The limit may be dynamic, as the limit for str<->int conversions.

This seems to be related to a more general problem of the `PyUnicode_Decode<ENC_NAME>Stateful` functions, where all the `Stateful` functions don't carry any state information across calls. This problem seems to be the root cause of several open issues, as well as a few closed ones. Currently, the non-`Stateful` (`PyUnicode_Decode<ENC_NAME>`) functions simply call the `Stateful` ones. 

Perhaps adding another level of function `PyUnicode_Decode<ENC_NAME>TrulyStateful` (ideally a better name) could be added. This function would take and mutate a `state` perameter, and therefore become actually stateful.

Hi Peter,

Thank you for opening this issue. I'd note that we had extensive discussions about the PDF documentation, spanning several months: https://discuss.python.org/t/101343/. Currently, the PDF archives are not well maintained, eg they do not meet the presentational standards I would expect of a technical manual.

We do continue to publish both the online HTML documentation, downloadable archives of the HTML documentation, and an EPUB document containing the entirety of the Python documentation. I would be curious as to which, if any, of these would be a suitable replacement for your needs, and if none, the reasons they're not suitable substitutes.

This isn't a decision I took lightly, and if there were a way to reintroduce PDFs without the significant maintenance burden I would gladly do so, but sadly it is not so.

I hope this provides some context as to the changes we've made.

Thanks,
Adam

I looked at both the HTML archive and the EPub. The EPub is basically all documents lumped together in one single file. It takes ages to load (with Calibre on Windows), and it is very slow to navigate. Paging up and down takes seconds. I dont see this with any other EPub documentation I have (and I have a lot!) To be more useful, it would need to be split like the PDF docs were: one file per document; and it needs to have proper metadata so as to be able to have multiple Python version EPub docs in the library and be able to tell them apart. Currently, the title is just "Python".

The HTML docs are not as easily navigable as the PDF and the EPub because they don't have a permanent TOC on the left pane; instead most of the time the TOC is embedded in the page itself. It's not easy to get an overview this way. And I prefer not to have to use my browser to read the docs; because most if not all of my other programming related docs is PDF. E.g. just look at the PostgreSQL documentation: they manage to do a beautiful and properly updated new PDF of ~3000 pages with each and every release; just like you used to do it up until now!

The Python PDFs were just perfect: nice TOC, beautifully layout and fonts, and they were more easily accessible by a screen reader and easier to do a full text search.

That the PDFs are now missing is, for me, a major regression. You have taken away from me what I was used to for many years, and what I loved because of the quality and accessibility.

I didn't notice the discussion that was going on re the removal. I'm just a user, so I'm not monitoring feature and development discussions; if I had noticed, I would have vehemently opposed the removal.

I feel that if you would make a survey among users, the majority of them would miss the PDF docs like I do. Please bring them back!

Right now, the sidebar navigation there doesn't have anything useful in it, and one has to scroll manually past a huge amount of "what's new in Python" subsections to get to the more-useful parts of the docs.

My default PDF viewer has collapsible sections in the TOC.  So when I first open it I get a view of only the top-level sections, but I can expand each one to get the next layer, and so on.  Adjusting the full TOC to mimic that behavior would make it more usable IMO.

Or there are smaller changes that might help: maybe reordering the TOC entries would help, and/or limiting things to one or two levels of sections, and/or probably other things we could think about.

I also didn't know that that page existed until right now, so maybe there's a way to make it more discoverable?  A sidebar link under the page's TOC to the global TOC?

> I'm not sure we need to create sym_new_list like sym_new_tuple or we just need `sym_new_type(ctx, &PyList_Type);`

For these, we just want to set the type. The symbolic tuple representation is a special case, since tuples are immutable. Tracking the values in a list is much harder, since the list can change in many different ways. For example:

```py
t = (a, b)
l = [a, b]
foo(t, l)
x = t[0]  # The JIT can prove that x is a.
y = l[0]  # l may have been mutated by foo, so we can't prove anything.
```

The symbolic tuple representation allows us to track symbolic values inside of a tuple, even if they aren't constant. For instance, if we later guard that `x` is an `int`, then the JIT has also proven that `a` is an `int` as well (and vice-versa!). We *may* choose to (very carefully!) track the contents of mutable containers or object attributes in the future, but in general this is much harder to do correctly, and pays off in fewer cases.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ---- Config (overridable via env) ----
PYTHON_VER="${PYTHON_VER:-3.14.2}"
PREFIX="${PREFIX:-$HOME/.local/python-${PYTHON_VER}}"
WORKDIR="${WORKDIR:-$HOME/build-python-${PYTHON_VER}}"
JOBS="${JOBS:-$(nproc)}"
INSTALL_DEPS="${INSTALL_DEPS:-1}"              # set to 0 to skip apt

TAR="Python-${PYTHON_VER}.tar.xz"

# ---- Functions ----
detect_ubuntu_2404() {
  if [[ -r /etc/os-release ]]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1091
    . /etc/os-release
    [[ "${ID:-}" == "ubuntu" && "${VERSION_ID:-}" == "24.04" ]]
  else
    return 1
  fi
}

install_deps() {
  [[ "${INSTALL_DEPS}" -eq 1 ]] || { echo "Skipping apt dependencies."; return 0; }

  echo "Installing build dependencies (requires sudo)..."
  if detect_ubuntu_2404; then
    echo "Detected Ubuntu 24.04 -> enabling ondrej/php PPA for libmpdec-dev"
    sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:ondrej/php || true
  fi

  sudo apt update
  sudo apt install -y \
    build-essential pkg-config wget ca-certificates xz-utils \
    libssl-dev zlib1g-dev libbz2-dev libreadline-dev libsqlite3-dev \
    libncursesw5-dev libncurses5-dev libffi-dev liblzma-dev tk-dev \
    libgdbm-dev libgdbm-compat-dev uuid-dev libzstd-dev libmpdec-dev \
    libxml2-dev libxmlsec1-dev
}

build_python() {

  fi

  tar -xf "${TAR}"

  popd >/dev/null
}

run_smoke_tests() {

  echo "Running failing pair: test_interpreters + test_struct"
  "${py}" -m test test_interpreters test_struct
}

# ---- Main ----

echo "Workdir: ${WORKDIR}"

build_python

I think the root of the problem lies in the fact that we're doing some hacky things to implement a singleton for `UNBOUND`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/5730fd50f7e5ef4d164a34466ee11e8ce9ba710d/Lib/concurrent/interpreters/_crossinterp.py#L41-L59

As this issue shows, these shenanigans are fragile. Ned has a great article on why singletons aren't a great idea in Python: [Singleton is a bad idea](https://nedbatchelder.com/blog/202204/singleton_is_a_bad_idea.html). That article seems to apply here, so I'm in favor of eliminating singleton enforcement entirely (and just defining `UNBOUND` as an `object()`, which would fix the problem), but I'm not one to make Eric's decisions for him.

I looked into the `dataclasses` cases. A `frozendict` is currently handled fine, but not exactly as a `dict`. However, the same is true for classes that behave like a mapping so maybe this is ok. A minimal example:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict, astuple

@dataclass
class A:
    d: dict
    f: frozendict


lst = []
d = {"a": lst, "b": lst}
a = A(d, frozendict(d))

at = astuple(a)  # runs fine
print(at)  # looks good
print(at[0]["a"] is at[0]["b"])  # False
print(
    at[1]["a"] is at[1]["b"]
)  # frozendict is handled by deepcopy, so this returns True

ad = asdict(a)  # runs fine
print(ad)  # looks good
print(at["d"]["a"] is at["d"]["b"])  # False
print(at["f"]["a"] is at["f"]["b"])  # True
```

So I've been trying various approaches and there are few issues:

- While I understand that the package is popular, it's not been updated since 2023 and doesn't officially support Python 3.14. 
- Making it a different attribute so that people can do whatever they want with their 'file' is also not a good idea because imapclient uses the super `shutdown()` which calls `self.file.close()`. So if we renamed the attribute, it would become `self._imaplib_file.close()` and the file created by imapclient would still be opened.
- Making it writable again is annoying because we really don't want to use that attribute actually. If a connection is open, then sock and file are set but need to be synchronized. When opening an SSL connection, we wrap the socket and recreate the file. This is also an issue in our current code where we should have closed the previous file before wrapping the socket. I'm not sure the destructor automatically closes the SocketIO object (that could be annoying!)

I'm inclined to actually not change anything and ask maintainers of `imapclient` to fix the library. However, I can make it writable again and document that using it is at their own risk. Fixing the synchronization issue is honestly not that interesting either since I prefer removing the attribute altogether in the future so a deprecation is better for Python 3.15. I'll restore the behavior for Python 3.14.

---

> Or rename the internal attribute (e.g., _imaplib_file) instead of shadowing a long-existing public attribute 

As per [PEP-8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#public-and-internal-interfaces), it's not a public attribute. Something that is _not_ documented is not considered part of the public API.

The language reference is currently silent as to whether or not an
iterator's next() method is looked up on every pass around a for loop,
or whether it is OK for an implementation to look the method up once at
the start of the loop, cache the result and call it again each time
around the loop without doing the lookup again.

The language reference should require implementations to follow
CPython's behaviour in this respect: the method should be looked up
again on each pass around the loop.

Why does  CPython behave that way?  Accident or justified decision?

Guido didn't actually say whether or not this was originally just an
implementation accident or a deliberate design choice - he just
indicated that this was a case where caching the bound method should be
disallowed because it could change the semantics of existing programs.

As per my reply in https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/99602#issuecomment-1353765784, we don't need the `tzdata` package. It exists as a way to support data lookup when system provided tzdata is not available. We don't actually need it to test the code that loads the tzdata that way, it can be mocked. The only reason to add it would be for an integration test, which I am under the impression it's not that common here, and I don't think it's really needed, especially considering the `tzdata` PyPI package just repackages the tzdata from IANA, the upstream, (https://github.com/python/tzdata/blob/master/update.py) and we already test with the system provided tzdata.

> For completeness, can you post one line saying why the much simpler solution "range(a).stop" is not accepted?

Because it is implementation detail. The range() function if it will be implemented in Python needs operator.index().

The main purpose of adding Python implementation of the operator module was to provide an implementation which can be used in alternative Python implementations (e.g. PyPy). The CPython itself doesn't use it. And now I doubt that such complicated implementation will be helpful.

Perhaps we need a builtin which exposes \_PyType_Lookup() at Python level.

Ah.  If that's the only reason, then that seems a bit like misguided effort...  For alternative implementations like PyPy and Jython, the "\_operator" module is definitely one of the simplest ones to reimplement in RPython or Java.  Every function is straightforwardly translated to just one call to an internal function -- that we need to have already for the rest of the language.

...but yes, it's very obvious that exposing \_PyType_Lookup() to pure Python is the right thing to do here.  This is a central part of the way Python works internally, after all.

Moreover, sorry about my previous note: if we started today to write PyPy, then it would be enough to have the pure Python version of operator.index(), based on the newly exposed \_PyType_Lookup().  With PyPy's JIT, there is no real performance loss.  Some of my confusion came from the fact that there \*would* be serious performance loss if we had to work with the pure Python looping-over-__mro__-and-fishing-in-__dict__ version.

A lot of this discussion has flown a rather unfortunate distance over my head, especially since I've barely had time to follow it.  But it looks to me like--given the number of other places that do the same thing as operator.index currently does--there needs to be a simple way to do the right thing somewhere accessible, which probably means a builtin.

On the other hand, it seems to me like 'a.\_\_index__()' \*should* be "the right thing" to do, but I get the feeling that making that so would be an astronomically huge change without much real benefit and lots of opportunities to break everything.  I suspect I'm also missing something fundamental in why it's not the right thing to do.

I think we should make this behave atomically because:

1) it's written so that it behaves atomically in the GIL-enabled build.
2) it should be relatively easy (... famous last words)
3) the motivation is a real bug report in user code

The problem is a combination of:

1) We lock the to-be-copied deque when `__copy__` is called (good!)
2) We iterate over the to-be-copied deque, which tries to lock both the iterator and the deque

That triggers the deadlock avoidance routine, which unlocks the deque before re-locking both the iterator and the deque. The time in between the unlock and re-locking allows another thread to modify the deque (which would not be allowed in the GIL-enabled build).

Given that we already have an optimization where we skip locking (directly) nested critical sections of the same object, and we order CRITICAL_SECTION2 locks by mutex address to avoid deadlocks (so the order of it/deque locking is already opaque to the caller) -- couldn't we just skip locking whichever lock in a CRITICAL_SECTION2 is currently locked in the (previous) top-most critical section?

> couldn't we just skip locking whichever lock in a CRITICAL_SECTION2 is currently locked in the (previous) top-most critical section?

For posterity, I figured out why this approach was initially taken. The `_sysconfigdata` module is found via `getpath.py` which bases it on the location of the source checkout and `pybuilddir.txt`. Unfortunately, to get imports to work from a checkout we mount the checkout to `/` in the WASI guest which makes the checkout location recorded via `./configure` be incorrect. As such, we need to use `PYTHONPATH` to manually include the build directory that `pybuilddir.txt` points at. And since we need to set `PYTHONPATH` for the host runner when we call `./configure` so it ends up in `Makefile`, we need to calculate the path to the build directory instead of getting to use `pybuilddir.txt`.

Currently we have unicodedata.name() which returns the formal character name of the character chr as per the second column in UnicodeData.txt from http://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/.

However, there are a few characters where the formal character name has spelling mistakes. Also, the control characters in the Basic Latin and Latin-1 blocks aren't really given meaningful character names. In one case, that of FEFF, the formal name ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE refers to a deprecated usage of the character (and the alternate name BYTE ORDER MARK refers to the recommended usage).

In all these cases, improved names are provided as stable aliases in NameAliases.txt from the same UNIDATA source. These are also part of the stable standard and are intended to alleviate the naming situation w.r.t. the above issues. For the stability, see: http://www.unicode.org/policies/stability_policy.html#Formal_Name_Alias

Hence it would be most useful if the unicodedata module would add an aliasedname() method with the same signature as name() to provide the official aliased name in the case of characters with aliases, and when a character does not have an alias, to provide the same output as name().

As of Py 3.3, unicodedata.lookup() already uses/supports NameAliases.txt for returning the character given the name. The present requirement is to use it for returning the name given the character.

Note that NameAliases.txt has abbreviated names for some characters (where the third column reads "abbreviation"). While these would be useful for lookup(), they would not be useful to be returned for aliasedname(). For instance, one would prefer to see "SPACE" returned for 0020 rather than "SP". So these entries should be disregarded for aliasedname().

Also, NameAliases.txt has multiple entries for some characters even after discarding the abbreviation entries. In these cases, the first entry should be used (for want of a better rule). It is presumed that these are provided in some order of preference.

It should be noted that discussion on this topic on the "unicore" (Unicode members) mailing list (on the thread "When normative aliases exist..." started 2014-01-21) indicates that the order of entries is subject to change although the entries themselves will not be removed. In this case, the first non-abbreviation entry may change. This is acceptable for the behaviour of aliasedname(). Also note that aliases may be defined in future. Thus the string returned by aliasedname() for a given character is not guaranteed to be the same, but whatever is returned by it will surely be valid to use with lookup(). Those who desire a single immutable name and do not require the improvements provided by the aliases should use name() and not aliasedname().

Finally, for extended support, a namealiases() function should return all the aliases together with their types, allowing the user full choice of the desired but official alias.

The attached code should clarify the required behaviour. (It is not a patch, just an illustration.)

AFAIK, the examples in https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html actually don't even show that `Sequence.index` must have 3 arguments despite https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Sequence indicating that `start` and `stop` are now supported in `index`.

The source code however says `Supporting start and stop arguments is optional, but recommended`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/7e4afe0d52d8dfb18a33bcaf0cadffd98c821402/Lib/_collections_abc.py#L1047-L1052

AFAICT, there is no strict guidelines on the meaning of `start` and `stop` (though we're full of incompatible signature violations, e.g., tuple is not a subtype of Sequence in the strict sense as it doesn't accept None for `stop`). Should we support them to be a sequence or not?

----

Personally, I'm in favor of supporting None because it could simplify the rendered signature and makes it simpler to use. However, one could argue that for `stop` it doesn't matter because it's the last parameter, so whether we write `x.index(i, None)` or `x.index(i, sys.maxsize)`, both can simply be `x.index(i)`. What's interesting however is that it allows consumers to be simplified as they won't need to handle a None end themselves (and they could avoid using a default being `sys.maxsize` for instance).

Note that support of start/stop arguments in `Sequence.index()` is recent change and it was breaking. Not all sequences support them, and very few of them support them as keyword arguments.

Adding support of `None` is very easy in CPython code. It is a little more in user code, but I do not propose to force this, and it is dwarfed by the need to support negative and out of range values.

I think I prefer option 2 (do not support None). It is supported in the `[...]` methods I believe as a result of `slice(...)`, but for the various methods `None` has unclear intent, and as you say could hide an error with an unexpected `None` value.

I think it would be better to advance multisignature support than use `None` as a 'nice' default. We could also revisit [`inspect.UNREPRESENTABLE`](https://discuss.python.org/t/30753) as a stop-gap for `help`/`pydoc` output, instead of changing the runtime behaviour.

It seems like **mimalloc** only uses an alignment on 4 bytes (32-bit) on 32-bit systems.

pymalloc uses an alignment on 8 bytes (64-bit) on 32-bit systems (extract of `Include/internal/pycore_obmalloc.h`):

```c
#if SIZEOF_VOID_P > 4
#define ALIGNMENT              16               /* must be 2^N */
#define ALIGNMENT_SHIFT         4
#else
#define ALIGNMENT               8               /* must be 2^N */
#define ALIGNMENT_SHIFT         3
#endif
```

By default, mimalloc uses an alignment of `MI_MAX_ALIGN_SIZE` which is 16 bytes by default. But memory allocations smaller than 16 bytes use a lower alignment. See https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc/issues/199 (old mimalloc issue).

The failing test uses `array.array("B")` and then calls `a.append(0)` which allocates only **4 bytes**. When using mimalloc, this allocation is only aligned on 4 bytes (32-bit), whereas an alignment on 8 bytes (64-bit) is expected by the test.

mimalloc provides allocation functions with an explicit alignment: https://microsoft.github.io/mimalloc/group__aligned.html The problem is that the Python C API (memory allocation functions) has no alignment parameter.

I think the wording is ambiguous. On my 64-bit system, `_Alignof(max_align_t)` is 16 bytes. These are the minimum alignments I saw with a bunch of allocators:

| Size | glibc | tcmalloc | jemalloc | mimalloc | snmalloc |
| ---: | ----: | -------: | -------: | -------: | -------: |
|    1 |    16 |        8 |        8 |        8 |       16 |
|    2 |    16 |        8 |        8 |        8 |       16 |
|    4 |    16 |        8 |        8 |        8 |       16 |
|    8 |    16 |        8 |        8 |        8 |       16 |
|   16 |    16 |       16 |       16 |       16 |       16 |
|   24 |    16 |       32 |       32 |       32 |       32 |

The C99 spec (sec 7.20.3) says of `malloc`:

> the pointer returned is suitably aligned so that it may be assigned so that it may be assigned to a pointer to any type and then used to access such an object [...] in the space allocated

so yeah, I guess it's somewhat ambiguous, and I read it wrong, not helped by the macOS manpages of `malloc` that say it's _always_ aligned for `max_align_t`.  The Linux manpages for malloc (at least on my current system) specifically say it only needs to be allocated for types that fit in the space, which feels like the _better_ choice in general (and the one that matches your table).

```py
from threading import Thread
import os
import select
import sys

STDIN_FD = sys.stdin.fileno()

def get_input():
    while True:
        rfds, wfds, efds = select.select([STDIN_FD], [], [])
        if not rfds:
            continue
        data = os.read(STDIN_FD, 100)
        data = data.decode()  # assume UTF-8
        print(f"stdin got data: {data!r}")
        if not data:
            break

t=Thread(target=get_input, daemon=True)

The issue is that the input() call in the daemon thread prevents the program from exiting. The threading documentation says the following about daemon threads:

> The entire Python program exits when no alive non-daemon threads are left.

While preventing the main thread from exiting would technically be consistent with the documentation, it is certainly not desirable behavior. Every other blocking function that I tested does not cause this issue, including sys.stdin.readline(). Using non-blocking input is not an equivalent substitute, as it either requires busy waiting or using select, as in @vstinner 's reply, which does not work on Windows.

You may close this issue, as it is technically correct behavior, but I do suggest that this is addressed since it is an unintuitive behavior.

There is a constant for this purpose:
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/1ddb41268997938d5f416e1ac98ae39cc3e81535/Python/gc.c#L1363-L1365

If ever you face performance issues and want to spot whether the gc could be the culprit, it is useful to know that this SCAN_RATE_DIVISOR is 10 and therefore, the incremental gc on the old generation will work by bunch of 1/(threshold1 * SCAN_RATE_DIVISOR). The fact that threshold1 default to 10 and the documentation says the collected old generation is inversely proportional to threshold1, so 1% with threshold 10 (without any additional information) makes the reader wonder whether there is a typo. 

From my perspective it is not clear why you use SCAN_RATE_DIVISOR instead of just passing threshold1=100 and compute 1/threshold1. I do not challenge this choice (I didn't even looked at the source code), I am just spotting possible user misunderstanding of the usage of threshold1 that could be fixed by saying that the computation is 1/(threshold1*10)

> From my perspective it is not clear why you use SCAN_RATE_DIVISOR instead of just passing threshold1=100 and compute 1/threshold1.

It is done for "compatibility", let me quote myself from another [issue](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/142115#issuecomment-3592974519):

> Before 3.14 we have default values for thresholds like (2000, 10, 10). This means that after 100 gc runs (young + middle) we run full collection.
> For incremental gc we changed meaning of the second threshold value, and this change documented:
> 
> > The fraction of the old generation that is collected is inversely proportional to threshold1. The larger threshold1 is, the slower objects in the old generation are collected. For the default value of 10, 1% of the old generation is scanned during each collection.
> 
> This means that for default values (2000, 10, 0) after 100 runs we do collection for whole heap like before 3.14.

If you have any problems with GC's performance, feel free to open such issues. On the other hand, it may be useful to build CPython with `Py_STATS` (`--enable-pystats`), and look at it. > The `__instancecheck__` hook was added for a specific reason, to support virtual subclasses and abstract base classes.  This was an *extension* of `isinstance`, not a replacement.  There was no intention to change core functionality of `isinstance(obj, cls)` returning `True` when `obj` is an actual instance of `cls`.  The new feature that was offered was the ability to return `True` for  duck typed objects. Currently (python 3.8.6, unidata_version 12.1.0) unicodedata.decomposition outputs an empty string for hangul syllable (codepoints in the AC00..D7A3 range) while the decomposition is not empty: it is always two characters (either a LV syllable and a T Jamo or a L jamo and a V jamo). This decomposition is dedicible algorithmically (se §3.12 of Unicode Standard). A python version of the algorithm is below (I don’t know C, so I can’t propose a patch). 

For each hangul syllable hs, I have used unicodedata.noramize to check that the NFC of the decomposition is indeed hs, that the decomposition is two codepoints long, that the NFD of both hs and the decompotsition coincide 

```py
def hangulsyllabledecomposition(c):
    if not 0xAC00 <= ord(c) <= 0xD7A3 : raise ValueError('only Hangul syllables allowed')
    dLV, T = divmod(ord(c) - 0xAC00, 28)
    if T!=0 : #it is a LVT syllable, decomposed into LV:=dLV*19 and T 
        return f'{0xAC00+dLV*28:04X} {0x11A7+T:04X}'
    else : #it is a LVT syllable, decomposed into L , V
        L, V = divmod(dLV,21)
        return f'{0x1100+L:04X} {0x1161+V:04X}'
    # Constants used:
    # 
```
==============
    # 0xAC00 : first syllable == 1st LV syllable 
    #                            NB: there is one LV syllable every 28 codepoints
    # 0xD7A3 : last Hangul syllable
    # 0x1100 : first L jamo
    # 0x1161 : first V jamo
    # 0x11A7 : one before the 1st T jamo (0x1148), since T=0 means no trailing
    #
    # (all number below restricted for modern jamos where this algorithm is relevant)
    # 19 : Number of L jamos (not used here)
    # 21 : Number of V jamos
    # 28 : Number of T jamos plus one (since no T jamo for LV syllable)

What about `dataclasses.replace()`? It will still work, right?

Yes, `dataclasses.replace()` still would have the typing problem but the 
bigger problem is that currently all `TypeVar`s on dataclasses are 
inferred as invariant, even if one never uses `copy.replace()` or 
`dataclasses.replace()`. You are right that even with `replace=False` one 
can still use `dataclasses.replace()` which would be potentially unsafe 
from a typing perspective, but that seems like a problem to solve later. 
(For example linters could warn against the use of 
`dataclasses.replace()`.)

It seems desirable to me to make `copy.replace()` behave safely from a 
typing perspective, regardless of what `dataclasses.replace()` is doing. 
It's actually really good that the `__replace__` protocol was added 
because now it's possible to individually decide which dataclasses should 
have the replace functionality and which shouldn't have. And we have 
found out that dataclasses shouldn't have this functionality if they want 
to have covariant type variables. So we can now handle this correctly.

`replace()` just creates an object with specified attributes, taking defaults from attributes of the specified object. It can potentially work with any object, unless it is a singleton. The practical problem is that in general we do not know the correspondence between constructor parameter names and attribute names. But not for dataclasses, for dataclasses `replace()` should always work.

Typing issues are issues of existing static type checkers, they should not affect the runtime behavior.

Argparse was written in Python 2 era and it firmly has the ethos of that era in its design.

The default value is not necessarily the same type as the results of `type=`.  There's nothing in argparse's design that fundamentally enforces this (it doesn't really think in terms of "types"). The default could be a sentinel value, a function, UUID instance, deque of million ints, etc... The `type=` mechanism is designed to cast and validate from user input, but the default doesn't necessarily have to be the same as result of `type=` mechanism.  

As you've mentioned, the peculiar exception is the `str` case which will get forced through the casting/validation mechanism. I think you can make an argument that the default value shouldn't be validated via `type=` mechanism. 

```python
from argparse import ArgumentParser, ArgumentTypeError, ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter
from pathlib import Path
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass

NOT_PROVIDED = object()

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int


def _validate_dir(sx: str) -> Path:
    px = Path(sx).expanduser()
    if not px.is_dir():
        raise ArgumentTypeError(f"{px} is not a directory")
    return px


def _validate_positive_integer(value: str) -> int:
    x = int(value)
    if x < 1:
        raise ArgumentTypeError(f"{x} is not a valid positive integer")
    return x

def to_parser() -> ArgumentParser:
    p = ArgumentParser(formatter_class=ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter)
    f = p.add_argument
    # It's odd the default value is not shown for some of these in --help
    f('-o', '--output', type=_validate_dir, default=NOT_PROVIDED)
    f('-d', '--dragons', default=deque(["alpha", "beta"]), nargs="+")
    f('-f', '--filter', default=[User("a", 1)], nargs="*", help="filter options", type=_validate_positive_integer)
    # this is peculiar. changing the default to a negative value will raise an exception.
    f('-n', "--number", default="1234", help="number options", type=_validate_positive_integer, nargs="+")
    return p
```

I propose this algorithm, starting with the simplest optimization: LOAD_FAST; POP_TOP -> _NOP, or constant propagation.
https://github.com/faster-cpython/ideas/issues/561#issuecomment-2323395424

## Design Required background knowledge: * Abstract interpretation. Recommended reading by me: Tutorial on Static Inference of Numeric Invariants by Abstract Interpretation (Antoine Miné). The complex relational abstract domains are not required knowledge. * Partial evaluation. Recommended reading by me/Mark: Partial Evaluation and Automatic Program Generation by Jones, Gomard and Sestoft). Further reading for tracing JITs: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1929501.1929508 Design: Mark's [PhD theses](https://theses.gla.ac.uk/2975/) showed that partial evaluation in Python is almost useless without specialization, which provides type information. I thus propose the following design: 1. Create a new PE pass in a new DSL file, with all its required data structures. 2. The new PE pass shall be run in lockstep fashion after the current types/specialization optimizer pass for each instruction. So it would be SPEC -> PE for every instruction. a. This is not new art, as PyPy already runs its analysis in lockstep fashion for every instruction. 3. The key innovation: this new PE pass would receive information **unidirectionally** from the specialization pass. a. We supply all the type information we already have in the first pass to the second pass. In the literature, this is known as the cardinal product of 2 abstract domains. The abstract domains we are combining are the types lattice and the "shape"/object one). The key benefit is to reduce duplicated code and also increase the power of the second domain. For example, to perform a scalar replacement of tuples, we would need to know anyways that it's a tuple of size n, a type that we already have information about in the types specialization pass. b. By defining them as two separate domains, we ensure that they remain conceptually separate and clear. 4. Testing. We shall have testing modes that allow us to switch off either pass, so that we can individually test the passes still. However, note that the PE pass is not much useful without type information anyways, so there might be no point switching off the types pass just to test the PE pass. 5. Goals. Start with simple things like object allocation removal of slice objects and tuples on the stack that don't escape. We can expand more later. We should discuss the design further and refine it. @reidenong is likely taking the initial implementation up. ### Future direction Currently, we just stick the guards onto the end of the trace during the final phase when the executor prepares for execution. Unfortunately, if we are to do more complicated optimizations, we will need to reconstruct state before bailing to the interpreter. Mainly, we need some way to say "this is the state we need to restore at X point of execution upon exiting", and write the instructions to restore that state then. Instead, the optimizer should be able to know what instructions it needs to emit to restore the state. We can have a "guard arena" that stores each guard fragment, so during uop optimization it should look like this: After that pass and during the prepare for execution pass, we merge the guard buffer and main trace into one single buffer, and insert the final _EXIT_TRACE and _DEOPT instructions for each guard fragment while doing so.

Python identifiers are in NFKC form; string method .isidentifier() returns true on strings that are not in that form.  In some contexts, these non-canonical strings will be replaced with their NFKC equivalent, but in other contexts (such as the builtins hasattr, getattr, delattr) they will not.


```pycon
>>> cha=chr(170)
>>> cha
'ª'

>>> cha.isidentifier()
True

>>> uc.normalize("NFKC", cha)
'a'

>>> obj.ª = 5
>>> hasattr(obj, "ª")
False
>>> obj.a
5
```
I don't see why that's invalid. "str.isidentifier()" returning True means Python will accept it as an identifier.

My preference would be for non_NFKC.isidentifier() to return False, but that may be a problem for backwards compatibility.

It \*may* be worth adding an asidentifier() method that returns either False or the canonicalized string that should be used instead.

At a minimum, the documentation (including docstring) should warn that the method doesn't check for NFKC form, and that if the input is not ASCII, the caller should first ensure this by calling str1=unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", str1)

```pycon

True
```

`str.isidentifier()` returns True if the string can be used as an identifier in Python source code. Id does not matter if it is not normalized -- the Python parser will normalize it. But you need also to check if it is a reserved keyword -- and the documentation already mentions this.

The check for 0 items in the C implementation is an optimization. The check for 0 items in the Python implementation would not be so cheap. It would add an overhead. For very large lists and sets, only 1 of 1000 `APPENDS` and `ADDITEMS` operations will have 0 items.

Other drawback is that an error in invalid pickle is not detected.

We could remove the check for 0 items, but then we need to change the pickling code so that it does not produce `APPENDS` and `ADDITEMS` with 0 items. This would also result in smaller pickle data, but it needs more complex code.
It does not actually complicates the code, all bits are already here, they just need some rearranging. And the Python implementation already guarantees this.

APPENDS and ADDITEMS with empty items were very rare, and now they will be never produced in normal circumstances (unless the collection was modified during pickling). #144950 ensures that an error is raised even for empty items in both implementations and adds more tests for similar cases. Although there is no validation for SETITEMS with empty items. Weird, but it's not worth it.

Longer:
.. method:: socket.sendfile(file, offset=0, count=None)

   Send a file until EOF is reached by using high-performance
   :mod:\`os.sendfile\` and return the total number of bytes which were sent.
   \*file* must be a regular file object opened in binary mode. If
   :mod:\`os.sendfile\` is not available (e.g. Windows) or \*file* is not a

Description

I took a deeper look (at the `_py_abc` implementation but I assume it is equivalent to the C impl) and came to the same conclusions as @zrothberg. In https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/92810#issuecomment-1166589468:

> If you are generating classes the bulk of which never get compared in any natural way them getting involved in their parents issubclass call is unintuitive at best. Frankly I am not sure I fully understand the intent of it. I presume its for registered calls but if it is not and the intent is to allow subclasses to specialize how they check then it should just be considered bugged.

It seems that while the current `_py_abc.ABCMeta.__subclasscheck__` implementation is inefficient with a lot of subclasses it is necessary. Looking at it step by step (ignoring the cache related logic):

- This is equivalent to an `issubclass(subclass, cls)` check without virtual classes involved:

    https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/00f0771e4dbd8c8b66b302ebc16bb21f5d46b304/Lib/_py_abc.py#L131-L134

- This:

    https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/00f0771e4dbd8c8b66b302ebc16bb21f5d46b304/Lib/_py_abc.py#L135-L139

    is necessary to support:

    ```python
    from abc import ABC

    class MyABC(ABC): ...

    class Test: ...

    MyABC.register(Test)

    issubclass(Test, MyABC)  # True
    ```

- This:

    https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/00f0771e4dbd8c8b66b302ebc16bb21f5d46b304/Lib/_py_abc.py#L140-L144

    is necessary (and is the source of the performance issues) to support:

    ```python
    from abc import ABC


    class MyABC(ABC): ...


    class MySubABC(MyABC, ABC): ...


    class Test: ...


    MySubABC.register(Test)

    issubclass(Test, MyABC)  # True
    ```

The last one seems really uncommon. So I think the only solution would be to try to optimize things while keeping the existing logic, which seems relatively hard.

What I propose instead would be a way to disable virtual subclasses, e.g. with a metaclass argument:

```python
class MyABC(metaclass=ABCMeta, allow_virtual_subclasses=False):  # default True, name TBD
    pass
```

If `allow_virtual_subclasses` is `True`, `ABCMeta.__subclasscheck__` essentially acts as a simple `cls in subclass.__mro__` check.

It creates the following class tree:
```
Root(ABC)
|
|- Class1
|\
| |- NestedClass1_1
| |- NestedClass1_2
| |- ...
| \- NestedClass1_3000
|
|- Class2
 \
  |- NestedClass2_1
  |- NestedClass2_2
  |- ...
  \- NestedClass2_3000

```

compairing classes which are a direct descendants or ancestors, like:
```python
assert issubclass(Class1, Root) is True
assert issubclass(Class2, Root) is True
assert issubclass(NestedClass1_1, Class1) is True
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_1, Class2) is True
assert issubclass(NestedClass1_1, Root) is True
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_1, Root) is True
```
takes very little time, as parent class already in `__mro__` of its subclass, and `True` is returned early:
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Lib/_py_abc.py#L132-L134
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Modules/_abc.c#L784-L791

But compairing classes which are not related to each other, like:
```python
issubclass(NestedClass2_1, Class1)
```
takes a lot of time, because this clause:
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Lib/_py_abc.py#L141-L144
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Modules/_abc.c#L800-L825
leads to compairing each class in inheritance tree with another class in this tree:
```python
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_1, Class1) is False
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_2, Class1) is False
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_3, Class1) is False
...
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_6000, Class1) is False

assert issubclass(NestedClass2_1, NestedClass2_1) is False
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_2, NestedClass2_1) is False
...
assert issubclass(NestedClass2_6000, NestedClass2_1) is False

...
# until all combinations are checked
```
This is effectively O(N^2) algorithm, where N is number of classes under ABCMeta, and all their children. For 6K classes it's about 36M comparisons, which takes ~25 seconds.
Worse than time complexity is a fact that each negative check adds entry to `cls._abc_negative_cache`, taking up a lot of RAM. Script above consumes ~3.3GB of RAM.

It is also possible to prevent breaking code like this:
<details>

```python
from abc import ABC

class Root(ABC): ...

class Class1(Root): ...

class Other: ...

Class1.register(Other)

assert issubclass(Other, Class1) is True
assert issubclass(Other, Root) is True  # fails without cls.__subclasses__()
```
</details>

by introducing a internal change to class registration mechanism:
<details>

```python
Class1.register(Other)
Root.register(Other)  # automatically call .register() for each ancestor implementing ABC

assert issubclass(Other, Class1) is True
assert issubclass(Other, Root) is True
```
</details>

This approach is implemented here: #131914.

## Caveats 

Solution above breaks code like:
```
from abc import ABC

class Root(ABC): ...

class Class1(Root):
  __subclasses__ = lambda: [Other]

class Other: ...

assert issubclass(Other, Class1) is True
assert issubclass(Other, Root) is True  # fails without cls.__subclasses__()
```
because `cls.__subclasses__()` calls are important here to get all class descendants.

Probably, introducing some mechanism for resolving only these `__subclasses__ = ...` parts, without iterating over the entire inheritance tree, could solve this as well.

BTW, I'm not sure that `__subclases__ = ...` override should be checked by `isinstance` or `issubclass` at all.

For example, this is not the case for non-ABC classes:
```python
class Root: ...

class Class1(Root):
  __subclasses__ = lambda: [Other]

class Other: ...

assert Root.__subclasses__() == [Class1]
assert Class1.__subclasses__() == [Other]

assert Class1.__mro__ == (Class1, Root, object)
assert Other.__mro__ == (Other, object)

assert issubclass(Class1, Root) is True  # in MRO
assert issubclass(Other, Class1) is False  # not in MRO
assert issubclass(Other, Root) is False  # not in MRO
```
So why should it be the case for ABCMeta? There are no tests for such cases in both `test_isinstance` and `test_abc`.

Github code search doesn't return any combination of `__subclasses__` with ABC/ABCMeta. Only custom metaclasses where `__subclasses__` is tracked manually:
https://github.com/search?q=language%3APython+%22__subclasses__+%3D%22&type=code&p=1

Note you can avoid the first entry from __mro__ since that's going to be the class you already registered. Not that it really matter in terms of performance.

pydantic's BaseModel uses ABCMeta only because this:
```python
from abc import ABCMeta

class BaseMeta(type):
    pass

class BaseModel(metaclass=BaseMeta):
  pass

class UserDefined(BaseModel, metaclass=ABCMeta):
  pass
```
fails with error:
```
TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases
```

Some users actually don't need ABCMeta `.register()` or `__subclasses__` handling at all, and the regular inheritance is just enough. There is a way to avoid these costly features by using custom metaclass (see https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/11669):
```python
from abc import ABCMeta

class CustomABCMeta(ABCMeta):
    # no .register(). no __subclasses__
    __instancecheck__ = type.__instancecheck__
    __subclasscheck__ = type.__subclasscheck__

class Root(metaclass=CustomABCMeta):
    pass
```

I've implemented 2 different solutions for this issue.

#131914 adds a recursion guard inside the `for scls in cls.__subclasses__()` clause, to avoid adding the checked subclass into either positive or negative cache of a _all_ subclasses in the class tree.
This drops memory usage from several GB to few MB for 5k+ class tree. But for `_py_abc` implementation it doesn't makes the `isinstance`/`issubclass` much faster - timing drops from 8us to 3us (13us -> 10us for py_abc), as this is still O(len(subclasses) * depth(subclass_tree)) algorithm for the first _uncached_ check.

#141171 disables `for scls in cls.__subclasses__()` completely by bubbling up `cls.register(subclass)` call into all parents of `cls`. As there is no need to dive deep into the subclass tree, subclass is added only to `cls` positive/negative cache instead of messing up with children class caches.
To avoid issues with explicit `__subclasses__ = ...` override mentioned in https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/92810#issuecomment-2818224223, I've added a check into `def __new__(...)` which detects presence of `__subclasses__` in class `__dict__` which enables this clause back (rare but possible case).
This also drops memory usage from several GB to just few MB for 5k+ class tree. But also it drops timing of `isinstance`/`issubclass` of from 8us to 0.2us, because the entire for loop and recursion is skipped, making an algorithm effectively a O(len(abc_registry)) for the first _uncached_ check. For simple cases like `Number.register(int); issubclass(int, Number)` it's actually O(1) because of `if subclass in cls._abc_registry:` check.

Probably explicit `__subclasses__ = ...` override should not be supported by ABCMeta at all - regular classes do not check it, and nested `self.__subclasses__()` is just an implementation detail which could be eliminated with #141171. But someone could already rely on this behavior...

Ok, it's false sharing between `tlbc_index` in `_PyThreadStateImpl` and the `_qsbr_thread_state` from a different thread. If you're unlucky, the tail end of `_PyThreadStateImpl` ends up in the same cache line as the beginning of the `_qsbr_thread_state` array.

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/895e83727d6d686ab7dd5494f3ccd52b0726502e/Include/internal/pycore_tstate.h#L86-L87

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/895e83727d6d686ab7dd5494f3ccd52b0726502e/Include/internal/pycore_qsbr.h#L72-L76

We have padding at the end of each `struct _qsbr_pad` to avoid false sharing with other entries within the array, but that doesn't prevent false sharing between the first entry in the array and other data.

I think we want to do two things:

1) Align the beginning of the array to 64 bytes. Since we use the PyMem_Raw allocator, I think we just over allocate by 64 bytes  and then align.

2) Pad the end of `_PyThreadStateImpl` so that we avoid potential false sharing with other data structures.

```py
import re

import keyword

```

We import `inspect` and `enum` and those are heavy modules.

The imports are as follows:

- You import _colorize means you import dataclasses and thus inspect.
- You import logging means you import traceback, and thus _colorize, and thus dataclasses and thus inspect.

Because of that, we slow down imports to logging. Compare:

```
$ python -S -X importtime -c 'import logging'
$ python -S -X importtime -c 'import sys; sys.modules["_colorize"] = object(); import logging'
```

Or more strikingly:

```
$ python -S -X importtime -c 'import traceback'
$ python -S -X importtime -c 'import sys; sys.modules["_colorize"] = object(); import traceback'
```

Outside of the import time improvements, most of the construction time in `dataclasses` is spent on the `exec` call to create all of the functions.

```python
from cProfile import Profile
from pstats import Stats
from dataclasses import dataclass

with Profile() as p:
    for _ in range(5000):
        @dataclass
        class Example:
            a: int
            b: str
            c: str
            d: list[int]
            e: dict[str, int]

    stats = Stats(p)
    stats.strip_dirs()
    stats.sort_stats("tottime")
    stats.print_stats(10)
```

One way to potentially make this faster in many cases would be to defer the generation of the methods using descriptors, only generating the methods that are actually used. I think typing issues are not a good reason to make inner classes public.

Create a protocol, and use it. This is the right way in dynamically typed programming languages like Python. Or just use non-public classes if you are not afraid that your code can break with future Python versions.

I'm alright with the protocol approach, however I think that should live in CPython. Python is exposing an interface here, so should be able to expose a machine readable variant of it too (which types essentially are, so type checkers know what contract user code should follow).

Exposing an interface does not mean that its implementation should be exposed. We could document that only the name becomes public (like we did for Action) and that it should be treated as a protocol (kinda) but if we were to do something within the stdlib, creating protocols would be better (though, it would come at some cost oj our side).

* Are reading CSV files which are about what Excel would produce with its default settings

or

* Know just what your format is, and can define the various parameters easily

I agree that the parameters are easily deduced for any one csv file after a
quick inspection. The reason I went searching for a good sniffer was that I
have \~2100 csv files of slightly different formats coming from different
sources. In some cases, a csv file is sent directly to me, other times it
is first opened in excel and saved, and other times it is copy-pasted from
excel into another location, yielding 3 variations on the formatting from a
single source. Multiply that by 8 different sources of data.

For hacking disparate data sources together, it is more interesting to have
a sniffer that works really well to distinguish among the most common
dialects of csv, than one that tries to deduce the parameters of a rare or
unknown format. I agree with you that it would be a rare case that the
format is completely unknown -- more likely, you know it is one of two or
three possible options and don't want to have to inspect each file to find
out which.

The header file pyconfig.h mishandles the \_POSIX_C_SOURCE and \_XOPEN_SOURCE preprocessor macros.

For older versions of Python, the pyconfig.h header specifies:

```c
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200112L
```


and:

```c
#define _XOPEN_SOURCE 600
```


For newer versions of Python, the pyconfig.h header specifies:

```c
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L
```


and:

```c
#define _XOPEN_SOURCE 700
```


The Open Group has documentation about these symbols:

http://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/xsh_chap02_02.html

In particular, the documentation states:

A POSIX-conforming application should ensure that the feature test macro \_POSIX_C_SOURCE is defined before inclusion of any header.

So, having a header file attempting to set \_POSIX_C_SOURCE violates this intention.

Yes, I am well aware that the Python documentation says to include Python.h before any standard headers are included.  However, this is still problematic.

In particular, it causes trouble for source code that wishes to include the Python headers and wishes to use declarations that are made visible by setting later values for \_POSIX_C_SOURCE and \_XOPEN_SOURCE.

I would suggest the pyconfig.h be updated to have something like this:

```c
#if !defined(_POSIX_C_SOURCE) || _POSIX_C_SOURCE < 200112L
#ifdef _POSIX_C_SOURCE
#warning Python expects -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200112L or later
#undef _POSIX_C_SOURCE
#endif
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200112L
#endif
```


and this:

```c
#if !defined(_XOPEN_SOURCE) || _XOPEN_SOURCE < 600
#ifdef _XOPEN_SOURCE
#warning Python expects -D_XOPEN_SOURCE=600 or later
#undef _XOPEN_SOURCE
#endif
#define _XOPEN_SOURCE 600
#endif
```

In `unicodedata`, the functions `lookup` and `name` have some bugs and inconsistencies.

`lookup` matches case-insensitively, except for the algorithmic names of Hangul syllables and CJK unified ideographs, which must be in all caps. The documentation does not explain how character names are fuzzily matched.

`lookup` accepts names like “CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-04E00”, where the code point has a leading zero.

`lookup` and `name` don’t implement rule NR2, defined in chapter 4 of Unicode, for Tangut ideographs’ names.

just hit the difference between `CJK UNIFIED IDEOGAPH-*`, `HANGUL SYLLABLE *` and other unicode names again:

```
>>> "\N{SNOWMAN}\N{SNOWmAn}\N{sNoWMAN}\N{snowman}"
'☃☃☃☃'
>>> # but:
>>> "\N{CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-3400}"
'㐀'
>>> "\N{cjk UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-3400}"
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    "\N{cjk UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-3400}"
                                    ^
SyntaxError: (unicode error) 'unicodeescape' codec can't decode bytes in position 0-29: unknown Unicode character name
```

It seems that general rule NR2 was only introduced in [Unicode 9.0.0](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode9.0.0/ch04.pdf), and initially it only described CJK unified ideographs, CJK compatibility ideographs and Tangut ideographs. In [Unicode 17.0.0](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-4/#G144161) it is also applied to Egyptian hieroglyphs, Khitan small script characters and Nushu characters. So, it makes sense to use some generic code, and maybe generate data tables or code from UnicodeData.txt.

Thank you for your report, @dscorbett, and for your PRs, @wismill and @SnoopJ. My apologies that it took so long to review them -- we have few Unicode experts -- but finally this was resolved.

3.13 and 3.14 will only accept the Tangut ideographs' names, but not produce them. 3.15 will also produce them.

Egyptian hieroglyphs, Khitan small script characters and Nushu characters were already supported, because their names were listed explicitly in UnicodeData.txt. But this gives us opprtunity for optimization, see #144882.

There is a bit more going on than just refcount contention. The code 
```
s = frozenset({1, 2, 3})
z in s
```
scales poorly in the FT build. 

* The reason is that the `z in s` is specialized to `_CONTAINS_OP_SET` which calls `_PySet_Contains` ([here](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Python/bytecodes.c#L2857)) which has a lock

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/0d76dccc3b4376ba075a1737f58809e3d83aaaa3/Objects/setobject.c#L2235-L2242

* A second reason is there might be refcount contention in `set_lookkey`

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/0d76dccc3b4376ba075a1737f58809e3d83aaaa3/Objects/setobject.c#L103-L110

The increment is there because `startkey` is a borrowed reference and the rich compare might remove `startkey` from the set. For a frozenset this cannot happen, so we can skip the incref/decref. For a frozenset we can also skip the guard `if (table != so->table || entry->key != startkey)`.

To address the issues we can either

* Make dedicated methods for frozenset (this requires some duplication of code and a new _CONTAINS_OP_FROZENSET bytecode)
* Add a quick check using `PyFrozenSet_CheckExact` at the appropriate places and act accordingly.

**Python 3.13 is not security-only** — it is the current active release branch that accepts bugfix commits. This means the fix is eligible for 3.13.x.

## Addressing "Is there an actual issue this caused?"

Yes. The reproducer is derived from a real-world tool — a network scanner using `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` with many workers. In production:

- Users press `Ctrl+C` once to stop the scan
- If the timing is right (which happens in practice with 100+ threads), a **single** `Ctrl+C` can land during `_PyImport_Cleanup`
- The burst approach in the reproducer simply increases the probability to make it reliably reproducible for testing

The key point: **this is not only an artificial scenario**. Any multi-threaded Python program using `ThreadPoolExecutor` that gets `Ctrl+C` during shutdown has a window where this can occur. The more threads, the wider the window.

## Addressing "blocking signals can be dangerous"

I agree that permanently blocking signals is problematic. However, the vulnerable window in `_PyImport_Cleanup` is very short. A more targeted approach could work:

- **Option A**: Temporarily block `SIGINT` only during the `sys.stderr = None` assignment in `_PyImport_Cleanup`, then restore. This is microseconds, not seconds.
- **Option B**: Instead of setting `sys.stderr` to `None`, set it to a minimal fallback writer that doesn't crash `PyErr_Display`. This avoids the signal-blocking question entirely.
- **Option C**: Make `PyErr_Display` handle `sys.stderr = None` more gracefully — suppress output instead of falling through to `_PyObject_Dump`.

None of these require blanket signal blocking.



## Addressing "_PyObject_Dump is designed as a fallback"

I understand `_PyObject_Dump` is intentionally a fallback, and I see it has been promoted to public API (`PyObject_Dump`) in 3.15 for debugging purposes.

However, the concern is not about the function's existence — it's about **when it gets triggered**. A user pressing `Ctrl+C` on a multi-threaded program is normal operation, not a debugging scenario. The fallback to `_PyObject_Dump` here means the normal error-reporting path is broken during a window that real users can hit.

The race condition in `_PyImport_Cleanup` exists across all current Python versions (3.12, 3.13, 3.14). This is not a version-specific issue — it's a fundamental signal safety gap in `Py_FinalizeEx`.

> Python 3.13 is not security-only — it is the current active release branch that accepts bugfix commits. This means the fix is eligible for 3.13.x.

I don't appreciate the use of ChatGPT because it makes false assertions like this -- just because a fix *could* be backported doesn't mean it will. Again, changing handling of `sys.stderr` or signals is invasive and not something to be taken lightly; there is a very real chance that changing this will break code that already relies on the `_PyObject_Dump` output. If this gets fixed, it will likely only be for the 3.15 release in October.

> The key point: this is not only an artificial scenario. Any multi-threaded Python program using ThreadPoolExecutor that gets Ctrl+C during shutdown has a window where this can occur. The more threads, the wider the window.

Okay, but why does the network scanner care? What is it doing that this behavior breaks?

> Option A: Temporarily block SIGINT only during the sys.stderr = None assignment in _PyImport_Cleanup, then restore. This is microseconds, not seconds.

I meant that blocking signals, even during this small window, is dangerous. SIGINT is a debugging tool on its own, so if something gets stuck here, we're removing the ability to debug it with CTRL+C.

> Option B: Instead of setting sys.stderr to None, set it to a minimal fallback writer that doesn't crash PyErr_Display. This avoids the signal-blocking question entirely.

Again, ChatGPT is wrong. `call_py_exitfuncs` and `_PyImport_Cleanup` no longer exist and have not existed since 3.9. `sys.stderr` is now simply cleared when clearing `sys.__dict__`. So, if we put a new object in there, it still has to be deallocated. There will always have to be a point where `sys.stderr` is `None` during finalization, or otherwise we're leaking memory. (We *could* make an immortal static object that prints to the C `stderr` stream, but is that really better than just using `_PyObject_Dump`?)

> Option C: Make PyErr_Display handle sys.stderr = None more gracefully — suppress output instead of falling through to _PyObject_Dump.

See [the Zen of Python](https://peps.python.org/pep-0020/): "Errors should never pass silently."

> The race condition in _PyImport_Cleanup exists across all current Python versions (3.12, 3.13, 3.14). This is not a version-specific issue — it's a fundamental signal safety gap in Py_FinalizeEx.

Python is generally not signal-safe, especially during finalization.

FWIW, we have this code in Mailman 3:

```py
class Mailbox(MMDF):
    """A mailbox that interoperates with the 'with' statement."""

    def __enter__(self):
        self.lock()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.flush()
        self.unlock()
        # Don't suppress the exception.
        return False
```

There is an ambiguity. What should the context manager do? Should it call a close() on exit (as the OP implies)? Or call lock() on enter and unlock() on exit as in Barry's example? Both behaviors look reasonable.

"In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess" and "Explicit is better than implicit". This is perhaps the reason why this feature is not implemented yet. Perhaps there were discussions about this in the past.

contextlib.closing() can be used for explicit requesting the first behavior. Maybe it's a time to add contextlib.locked() or something like.

Currently, the implementation of .close() methods call flush() and
unlock() if it's needed.

About the ambiguity for the enter call, I think the context manager
should provide access to Mailbox, not a lock. If a lock is needed, we
could imagine another context manager:
with mailbox.Mailbox as mbox:
   #read messages, ...
   with mbox.lock():
      #actions that need lock

Do you think it's better?

I don't know the mailbox API particularly well, but the fact the object offers all three of lock(), unlock() and close() as methods does imply a fair bit of inherent ambiguity.

One option would be to offer a module level "mailbox.locked()" API to handle the lock/unlock case, and then have native context management on the mailbox itself that was akin to "contextlib.closing".


(Note regarding contextlib.locked(): the reason we don't currently have that is because there's no consistent protocol for locking method names. acquire()/release() and lock()/unlock() would be the most popular pairings, so we could technically offer both "contextlib.acquired()" and "contextlib.locked()", but the duplication still seems a bit dubious to me)

It's possible that the Mailman example can just assume that the mailbox will be flushed and unlocked on \_\_exit__(), so it could just call .close().  Then the question is whether entering the CM should lock the mailbox.  The two cases are:

1. It doesn't, so you'd have to do:

```py
with mbox(...) as mb:
    mb.lock()
    # ...
```


2. It does, so if for some reason you didn't want the lock, you'd have to:

```py
with mbox(...) as mb:
    mb.unlock()
```


We *could* add a `lock` argument to the constructor to take the ambiguity away.  But I would claim that it doesn't make much sense to acquire an mbox in a CM and *not* lock it.  The idiom says to me "I want to do things to the mbox, exclusively, and if that requires locking it, JFDI".

So I would argue that the \_\_enter__() should acquire the lock by default if the underlying mailbox supports it.

A well known anti-pattern in Python is use of re.match when you meant to use re.search.

`re.fullmatch` was added in 3.4 via https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/60407 for similar reasons.

`re.prefixmatch` would be similar: we want the re.match behavior, but want the code to be obvious about its intent.  This documents the implicit `\A` (or `^` when not `re.MULTILINE`) in the name.

The goal would be to allow linters to ultimately flag `re.match` as the anti-pattern when in 3.12+ mode.  Asking people to use `re.prefixmatch` or `re.search` instead.

This would help avoid bugs where people mean `re.search` but write `re.match` and would ease the cognitive load at code review time by encouraging explicit code without detailed specific Python `re` domain knowledge on the reviewers part.

The implementation is trivial.

This is **not** a decision to deprecate the widely used in 30 years worth of code's re.match name.  That'd be painful and is unlikely to be worth doing.

Discussion in https://discuss.python.org/t/add-re-prefixmatch-deprecate-re-match/105927

I seen a code which uses re.search() with anchor ^ instead of re.match(), but I never seen a code which uses re.match() instead of re.search(). It just won't work unless you add explicit ".\*" or ".\*?" at the start of the pattern, and it is a clear indication that re.match() matches the start of the string.

My point is that re.match is a common bug when people really want re.search.

re.prefixmatch makes it explicit and non-confusing and thus unlikely to be used wrong or misunderstood when read or reviewed.

The term "match" when talking about regular expressions is not normally meant to imply any anchoring as anchors can be expressed within the regex.  Python is relatively unique in bothering to have different methods for a prefix match and an anywhere match.  (We'd have been better off without a match method entirely, only having search - too late now)

> It just won't work unless you add explicit ".\*" or ".\*?" at the start of the pattern

But think of when regexes are used for validating input. Getting it to "just work" may be over-permissive validation that only actually checks the beginning of the input. They're one missed test case away from a crash or, worse, a security issue.

This proposed name change would help make the function behavior obvious at the callsite. In the validator example, calling "prefixmatch" would stand out as wrong to even the most oblivious, documentation-averse user.

> My point is that re.match is a common bug when people really want re.search.

While I think better distinguishing the interfaces is a nice-to-have for usability, I think it has more absolute benefit to correctness. Again, confusion around the semantics of "match" were the motivation for adding "fullmatch" in the first place but that change only went so far to address the problem: It's still too easy to misuse the existing "match" interface and it's not realistic to remove it from the language. A new name would eliminate this class of error at a very low cost.

What do other APIs in widely used languages do with regex terminology?  We appear to be the only popular language who anchors to the start of a string with an API named "match".

libpcre C: uses "match" to mean what we call "search" - https://www.pcre.org/current/doc/html/pcre2_match.html

Go: Uses "Match" to mean what we call "search" - https://pkg.go.dev/regexp#Match

JavaScript: Uses "match" to mean what we call "search" - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/match

Java: Uses "matches" (I think meaning what we call fullmatch?) - https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/util/regex/Pattern.html

C++ RE2: explicit "FullMatch" and "PartialMatch" APIs - https://github.com/google/re2 

Jave re2j: uses "matches" like Java regex.Pattern - https://github.com/google/re2j 

Ruby: Uses "match" as we do "search" - https://ruby-doc.org/core-2.4.0/Regexp.html

Rust: Uses match as we do "search" - https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/

I am not convinced. What are examples of using re.match() instead of re.search()? How common is this type of errors?

There are perhaps many millions of scripts which use re.match(), deprecating re.match() at any time in future would be very destructive, and keeping an alias indefinitely would only add more confusion.

From an explicit is better than implicit standpoint I still think this is a good idea. **Even if never actually deprecating and removing `re.match`**

Just promoting use of the explicit spelling of the API call in documentation and examples should be benificial to the ecosystem as a whole. Code analyzers (pylint, etc) could then suggest `prefixmatch` as more explicit when it finds an `re.match` call.

_(I edited the opening message to make it more clear, yay markdown)_

For anyone else who just learned about `re.fullmatch()`, the docs are at https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#re.fullmatch .

The naming of `re.match()` is rather unfortunate. I don't know how often the mistake is made of using the wrong function/method, but I'm sure it's more than non-zero. I'm +0 on the alias.

I'm also not convinced :thinking:

> A well known anti-pattern in Python is use of `re.match` when you meant to use `re.search`.

If people are not aware that `re.prefixmatch` exists and/or of the behavior of `re.match`, then they will keep using `re.match`, possibly incorrectly.  Many are not aware of `re.fullmatch` either.

> The goal would be to allow linters to ultimately flag `re.match` as the anti-pattern when in 3.12+ mode. Asking people to use `re.prefixmatch` or `re.search` instead.

This will only reach people that use such linters, similarly to how a warning in the docs only reaches people that do read the docs (and notice the warning).  Both could be applied to mitigate the problem, but neither are definitive solutions, and adding a new function has a cost.  So, unless I'm missing something, the addition will only serve to provide a more explicit alternative for the subset of users that use a linter or that are aware of the function and decide to use it.

However, an alternative already exist: they could just use `re.search` in most cases[^1], possibly with a regex like `^...` (if they want the `re.match` behavior) or `^...$` (if they want the `re.fullmatch` behavior).  Technically linters could already suggest that (even though it might be a tougher sell than an explicit function).

> This would help avoid bugs where people mean re.search but write re.match and would ease the cognitive load [...]

It might also increase it though, since now people will have to decide whether to use `search`, `match`, `fullmatch`, `prefixmatch` and wonder about their differences, and the fact that two have different names but the same behavior is potentially confusing (especially if they end up being used together while updating old code).  Some might also wonder why there is no `suffixmatch`, and possibly propose it.

[^1]: there are some difference when `re.MULTILINE` is used: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#search-vs-match

> the addition will only serve to provide a more explicit alternative for the subset of users that use a linter or that are aware of the function and decide to use it.

Yes. Exactly! That is the entire point. To allow those who realize that being explicit reduces the cognitive correctness burden for all developers working in their codebase, huge or small, to do so.

> an alternative already exist: they could just use re.search in most cases, possibly with a regex like ^... (if they want the re.match behavior) or ^...$ (if they want the re.fullmatch behavior).

`^` is not the logical re equivalent to `.match` behavior. There's a different backslash letter thing that is "start of string" which virtually nobody knows off the top of their head so would be more bewildering. Again, it's about the ease of being explicit. It is obvious what behavior `.prefixmatch` implies. It is not at all obvious that `.match` does that given that one talks about regular expression "matches" in English all the time as a matter of terminology and **never** means "oh, only at the start of the string" in that discussion context. Python has a mismatch with real terminology by differing from other major regex sporting languages/libraries used across the industry here. This offers a way out.

Without disruption of removing a very widely used API.

I'm just seeking to enable being explicit in code instead of requiring a code comment saying `# prefixmatch` upon every occurrence of `.match(...)` in code as a preventative measure. Practicality beats purity.

I don't see an added cognitive burden here from a new explicit method name. Nobody needs lookup `prefixmatch`, it's behavior is there in the name. If it's existence causes them question reality and lookup `match`, they'll learn something from the suggestion not to use that API name and perhaps eventually modernize their code.

I would not have filed this feature request if this were not a repeated source of bugs or confusion from those new to Python at work where people regularly use more than one programming language.

Our old terminology has been outvoted by JavaScript, Golang, Rust, and libpcre. We should adapt by allowing developers to be readably explicit about their intent.

I have yet to see an example of mistakenly using `re.match()` instead of `re.search()`. `re.search()` can be mistakenly used instead of `re.match()` or `re.fullmatch()`, I seen more than one examples of it, but not vice versa. I can also expect that `re.match()` is used instead of `re.fullmatch()` in a number of cases, mostly in a code that predates `re.fullmatch()`.

I think there is a problem with an initial premise about  "a well known anti-pattern".

We have a habit of removing long deprecated features in Python. For sure, if something is deprecated, it will be removed in 8 or 12 years, even if it is a simple alias. Forcing people to rewrite tons of working code for stylish reason does not look as a worthy goal to me.

I think our disconnect is merely the difference between samples: "you're is not seeing it" and "my colleagues who routinely do code reviews for hundreds of people sometimes new to Python do see it" are both true statements.

There is a good case to be made that we as a project should provide automated code transformers with every Python release that can be used to migrate source code towards the preferred more modern thing _when feasible_ (and encourage changes to be such that this _is_ feasible). Past examples: `2to3` did this where it could (limited) and ultimately is what lies behind the `modernize` tool which kept that torch lit and is more useful.

But I wouldn't want to _block_ this mere preferred more explicit name alias going in until such tooling to handle a decade later _potential_ deprecation of the old name being available. They're separate requests.

We recently had a few discussions related to this, including in the last [docs-community meeting](https://github.com/python/docs-community/pull/97#discussion_r1443637408) or on Discord.
The relevant bits are:
* Adding more examples is generally a good idea.  Depending on the context, it can be done inline, at the bottom of the page in an "Examples" section, or as a separate page.
* There's been some discussion about using collapsible sections (see the [issue linked above](https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx/pull/10532) by @AA-Turner).  Using `.. raw::` is probably not the right way to go, since there are already extensions that provide the feature.  However these are not compatible with all builders, so we can't just use them easily without a fallback for the other builders.

Until a better solution for collapsible sections is found, and if adding more example inline it's not desirable for the `str` methods, it might be better to just add the examples at the bottom of the page (like I did for [the `str.format` docs](https://github.com/python/cpython/commit/d2191e04a490b8bc43917a18604dde6a626aa7aa#diff-0b97370177394f7730fc5e3c6cd7eb2cd4878781d8d8509452caefc2cd69fc5dR474)) or possibly in a separate page (this needs a broader discussion though, especially if a similar approach gets adopted for builtin functions and possibly other pages).

I think we can make it thread safe with atomics, basically create a exchange loop and only initialize it if it is not initialized already. 

Something like this should work:


```diff
diff --git a/Include/datetime.h b/Include/datetime.h
index ed36e6e48c8..17c85b19e11 100644
--- a/Include/datetime.h
+++ b/Include/datetime.h
@@ -197,7 +197,15 @@ typedef struct {
 static PyDateTime_CAPI *PyDateTimeAPI = NULL;
 
 #define PyDateTime_IMPORT \
-    PyDateTimeAPI = (PyDateTime_CAPI *)PyCapsule_Import(PyDateTime_CAPSULE_NAME, 0)
+    do
+    {
+        PyDateTime_CAPI *capi = (PyDateTime_CAPI *)PyCapsule_Import(PyDateTime_CAPSULE_NAME, 0); \
+        if (capi && _Py_atomic_load_ptr(&PyDateTimeAPI) == NULL) { \
+            PyDateTime_CAPI *expected_api = NULL; \
+            _Py_atomic_compare_exchange_ptr(&PyDateTimeAPI, &expected_api, capi); \
+        }
+    } while (0)
+
 
 /* Macro for access to the UTC singleton */
 #define PyDateTime_TimeZone_UTC PyDateTimeAPI->TimeZone_UTC

```

This is the prototype of sem_clockwait():
```
#if __BIONIC_AVAILABILITY_GUARD(30)    
int sem_clockwait(sem_t* _Nonnull __sem, clockid_t __clock, const struct timespec* _Nonnull __ts) __INTRODUCED_IN(30);
