This isn't a bug. 

Super is a proxy object. For this one `super().__call__()` super is looking up Foo's (i.e., the parent's) `__call__` explicitly, so that makes sense that it works. For this one `super()()` it is looking up `type(super()).__call__)` and `__call__` doesn't exist on `super()` itself (only `__call__` on the actual object Super is proxying exists). Actually this is consistent with all the dunder methods. `len(super())` doesn't work even if the parent has `__len__`. 

Some other languages allow this! But I think for Python, allowing `super()()` would require the cpython super type to implement maybe some sort of dynamic dispatch at runtime to lookup the next class in the Method Resolution Order. But I am no expert on that, so only speculating that I think it would be a major bit of work.

I was also initially surprised to learn that `super()` was intentionally designed this way!
What you observed is [documented](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#super) and correct behavior:

> Note that [`super()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#super) is implemented as part of the binding process for explicit dotted attribute lookups such as `super().__getitem__(name)`. It does so by implementing its own [`__getattribute__()`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__getattribute__) method for searching classes in a predictable order that supports cooperative multiple inheritance. Accordingly, [`super()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#super) is undefined for implicit lookups using statements or operators such as `super()[name]`.

It's likely that many people stumbled across this in the past, e.g. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55992797/using-super-with-getitem-versus-subscript.

You could raise your idea at https://discuss.python.org/. I'd assume changing how `super()` works now on such a fundamental level would require a [PEP](https://peps.python.org/pep-0001/).

Having said that, I think the only thing we could potentially do in the near future is provide more helpful errors for our users:

```diff
-super()()  # TypeError: 'super' object is not callable
+super()()  # TypeError: super() objects are not callable. Use super().__call__() instead.

-super()[42]  # TypeError: 'super' object is not subscriptable
+super()[42]  # TypeError: super() objects are not subscriptable. Use super().__getitem__() instead.
```

```python
import http.server
import time
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

PORT = 8000
API_URL = f"http://localhost:{PORT}/api"


class RESTRequestHandler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        return http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler.__init__(self, *args, **kwargs)

    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path.startswith("/api/"):
            print("INNER path")
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            response = '{"a": 123}'.encode()
            print("... INNER response", time.perf_counter() - t0)
        else:
            print("OUTER path")
            t0 = time.perf_counter()

            # get path to inner
            _, _, *path = self.path.split("/")
            inner_url = f"{API_URL}/{'/'.join(path)}"

            # call inner
            request = Request(inner_url)
            response_raw = urlopen(request)
            response = response_raw.read()
            print("... OUTER response", time.perf_counter() - t0)

        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(response)


def rest_server(port):
    http_server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("", port), RESTRequestHandler)
    print(f"Starting HTTP server at port {port}")
    try:
        http_server.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        print("Stopping HTTP server")
        http_server.server_close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rest_server(PORT)
```

While investigating poor HTTP read performance I discovered that reading all the data from a response with a content-length goes via \_safe_read, which in turn reads in chunks of at most MAXAMOUNT (1MB) before stitching them together with b"".join. This can really hurt performance for responses larger than MAXAMOUNT, because
(a) the data has to be copied an additional time; and
(b) the join operation doesn't drop the GIL, so this limits multi-threaded scaling.

I'm struggling to see any advantage in doing this chunking - it's not saving memory either (in fact it is wasting it).

To give an idea of the performance impact, changing MAXAMOUNT to a very large value made a multithreaded test of mine go from 800MB/s to 2.5GB/s (which is limited by the network speed).

The 1 MiB limit was added for bpo-1296004; apparently some platforms were overallocating multiple buffers and running out of memory. I suspect the loop in "\_safe_read" was inherited from Python 2, which has different kinds of file objects. The comments suggest it does partial reads.

But the Python 3 code calls "socket.makefile" with "buffering" mode enabled by default. I agree it should be safe to read the total length in one go.

bpo-1296004 is too old (512MB RAM machine!) and I can not confirm it.

But I think it was caused by inefficient realloc() in CRT.

See https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/6c52d76db8b1cb836c136bd6a1044e85bfe8241e/Lib/socket.py#L298-L303

\_fileobject called socket.recv with remaining size.
Typically, socket can't return MBs at once.  So it cause:

1. Large (at most `amt`, some MBs) string (bytes) are allocated. (malloc)
2. recv is called.
3. _PyString_Resize() (realloc) is called with smaller bytes (typically ~128KiB)
4. amt -= received
5. if amt == 0: exit; goto 1.

This might stress malloc and realloc in CRT.  It caused fragmentation and MemoryError.

\---

For now, almost everything is rewritten.

In case of \_pyio, BufferedIOReader calls RawIOBase.read().  It copies from bytearray to bytes.  So call only malloc and free.  Stress for realloc will be reduced.

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/50866e9ed3e4e0ebb60c20c3483a8df424c02722/Lib/_pyio.py#L586-L591

In case of C \_io module, it is more efficient.  It allocate PyBytes once and calls SocketIO.read_into directly.  No temporary bytes objects are created.

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/50866e9ed3e4e0ebb60c20c3483a8df424c02722/Modules/_io/bufferedio.c#L1632
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/50866e9ed3e4e0ebb60c20c3483a8df424c02722/Modules/_io/bufferedio.c#L1658
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/50866e9ed3e4e0ebb60c20c3483a8df424c02722/Modules/_io/bufferedio.c#L1470

Additionally, \_safe_read calls fp.read() multiple times to handle EINTR.
But EINTR is handled by socket module now (PEP-475).

Now the function can be very simple.

Hi all. As the original subprocess module author, I'm a bit concerned over the expansion of the API. The number of arguments for the subprocess.Popen constructor is, to be honest, crazy. I am grateful for all work and bugfixes that has been done over the years, but the API is now quite far from the my original vision of a "small and clean API", which was the reason to "start from scratch", thus create the subprocess module. 

Removing preexec_fn and then adding additional arguments for cases where preexec_fn was used will further contribute to the "bloat" of the API, if I may use that word. 

I do understand the technical difficulties, but as always there are multiple alternatives. Better documentation as well as https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/82616#issuecomment-1093843959 are very interesting, as I see it.

Major kudos for its creation @astrand! Your work _largely_ succeeded! If it had not, it would've needed replacing again. =)

The original overall `subprocess` public API design was sound with one major exception: `preexec_fn=` was a conflicted with the existence of threads, thus why I label it as a fundamentally flawed feature.  Yet its existence also allowed for a lot of use cases that were otherwise unimplemented by subprocess and would've resulted in people coming up with even worse custom (read: buggy x1000) workarounds. So despite the problem, please don't consider this a criticism. It made the most sense at the time.

The remaining conundrum:

A library using the `subprocess` API with `preexec_fn=` is often not be owned by the same people owning code elsewhere in a broader application that uses threads. Both code owners believe they are right to do what they did. Afterall, they were just using documented public APIs with an expectation that they just work thanks to Python. Python programmers are often operating at a high level and not expected to need to know low level system programming details for what _appear_ to them to be normal mundane tasks like spawning a process or using threads.

If told they cannot expect do either they will have no good options that satisfy their needs. Their mere existence of both within the same process is the source of conflict. Use of threading is far more important to the world than realistic `preexec_fn=` use cases, thus nobody is advising _"nobody should use threads, a minority of people won't be able to do these esoteric things with child processes easily!"_. 😄 

In absence of ways to replace the functionality people use it for, `preexec_fn=` continues to exist, just with the giant warning about the random deadlocks that _will_ happen to end users of such unfortunate applications when the entire application stack is not tightly controlled.

Thus our dirty plethora of options added to replace many common things people were using preexec_fn= for.  Those also _greatly_ increase subprocess launching performance (done in C, vfork can be used, etc).  We've provided for some common cases. More exist. There is no way for us to predict and provide everything.

This is the largest detractor to "small and clean" that I hear users complain about today. It is true! But most people do not need these options in daily life. So that is perhaps best considered a documentation organization issue.

Stepping back from a **"What do users actually need?"** point of view, nothing has provided that:
 * Users need to be able to make subsets of a pretty long set of possible system calls with options before the ultimate child process is `exec`'d.
 * Users want doing that to perform well.
 * It is not possible to use arbitrary Python code and meet _both_ of the above two constraints.

Idea from above: Launching an intermediate Python interpreter process to run the preexec_fn code.

This is a good idea in terms of code compatibility. It would add a large Python interpreter startup time to the child process launch. But functionality wise it would work and the caveat can be documented. It also requires that a `sys.executable` interpreter binary to launch exists (excluding users of embedded Python, and possibly users running under an emulator? A deliberate choice we could make).

Brainstorming further Idea: A smaller binary to execute as the intermediate is one possibility. A microscopic tiny Python-ish interpreter with a restricted set of APIs (no import capability, presume `os` and `sys` exist, etc) sufficient to _just_ allow the kinds of system calls people need to make? I don't like the complexity, but it'd be entertaining to see how feasible this is. People can already manually use things like `/bin/sh` for some fraction of pieces of this concept today (very system dependent).

@gpshead thanks for your comments. preexec_fn is just a way to execute code between fork and exec, so as far as I can tell, the problem is exactly the same if you manually code fork() and exec() and some code in between. I assume that neither fork() nor exec() will be removed from the Python API, so why should preexec_fn be removed? As I understand it, Python 3.12 already has a mechanism in place to raise a DeprecationWarning if threads are detected. Why not use the same approach for preexec_fn?

I haven't looked too much into typing module, so take this with a grain of salt, but my understanding is that TypedDict is a special construct (as the first sentence in the docs defines it), which can be used as a base. I think most users would consider something a kind of a class if it can be inherited from by a user-defined class, so this classification in the docs is useful.

Normally functions can't be used as a base of course. There's no "inheritable from" abc or anything like that and functions are not inherited from "function type". You generally don't care if something is a function, you care if it's a callable and test for that with `callable()`.

So in a sense a function is the most inherently duck typed object in Python.

The only way for a specific check of a function type is AFAIK type(known_function) == type(myobj), but this type of checking is discouraged.

So static checkers that run into a problem with this are probably assuming too much about what a function is or should be in Python.

To sum up, TypedDict is a kind of a construct between a class and a function that's more usefully documented as, and used as, a class. The docs make it very clear that it's not your usual, run of the mill class.

TypeDict is a callable, it can be used as

```py
    Point2D = TypedDict('Point2D', x=int, y=int, label=str)
```


It can also be used as a base in class definition, but is is not a class itself. It does not occur in \_\_bases__ of the created class, and it cannot be used in isinstance() and issubclass() checks. It is just yet one weird way to customize class creation.

I agree that documenting it as class is not correct. Perhaps it should be declared as a function (with specifying its signature when used as a function) and referred with the :data: role.
Actually most names defined in typing are no longer classes.

One other consideration is the increase in size of inline caches necessary to store the type information and possible pointers.
To specialize for a method `__dunder__` we need a version number for the guard and a pointer to the `__dunder__` function.
Rather than put the pointer to the function inline we can cache it on the class, as we already do for `__getitem__` and `__init__` storing them in the class's `_specialization_cache`. If we expect specializations to be overwhelmingly builtin classes, a single 16bit cache is sufficient, but we will generally need a 32 bit (2 code units) cache.


Family    |   Current space in cache | Additional space needed for version
 ---- |  ---- |  ---- 
BINARY_OP | 4 | 0
CALL | 3 | 0
FOR_ITER | 0 | 1*
LOAD_ATTR | 8 | 0**
STORE_SUBSCR | 0 | 2
COMPARE_OP | 0 | 2
TO_BOOL | 2 | 0
CONTAINS_OP | 0 | 2

*We expect that most if not all iterators written in Python will be generators.
** No need to store the method in the `_specialization_cache` as there is space to store in inline

These are the specializations I think we should add to start with:

Family    |    `__dunder__` in Python | `__dunder__` in C 
 ---- |  ---- |  ----
FOR_ITER | FOR_ITER_PY_DUNDER | FOR_ITER_GENERIC 
CALL | CALL_PY_DUNDER | (already exists) 
LOAD_ATTR | (already exists) | LOAD_ATTR_GENERIC 
TO_BOOL | TO_BOOL_PY_DUNDER | TO_BOOL_GENERIC 
STORE_SUBSCR | STORE_SUBSCR_PY_DUNDER  | STORE_SUBSCR_GENERIC 
CONTAINS_OP | CONTAINS_OP_PY_DUNDER  | CONTAINS_OP_GENERIC 


We can leave `BINARY_OP` and `COMPARE_OP` for later, as they need more complex table-based approaches.

It should be possible to disable local events, and disabling is specific to the location passed to the callback.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.monitoring.html#local-events
How would you implement that?

Or do you want to make `PY_UNWIND` its own category, that can be turned on or off per code objects, but cannot be disabled?

If we are breaking the distinction between "local" meaning specific to a location and can be disabled, and "local" meaning can be turned on or off per code object, then we might as well make all events "local" in the second sense.

> It should be possible to disable local events, and disabling is specific to the location passed to the callback. https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.monitoring.html#local-events How would you implement that?

My understanding is that `DISABLE` is intended for those local events that can trigger at multiple locations. It can be used to fine-tune the events that the user wants to trap (e.g. just a sub-set of all the lines within a code object, or certain return statements). `PY_UNWIND` is obviously an event that is not _local_ in the sense of coming from a certain bytecode offset. However, one might argue that the event itself happens when the execution has reached a certain offset, so it (and in fact _any_ event) is local in this other sense. But because these events do not instrument the bytecode, they cannot be `DISABLE`d like other local events.

> Or do you want to make `PY_UNWIND` its own category, that can be turned on or off per code objects, but cannot be disabled?

Because as of now all local events require instrumentation, I would be more inclined to reflect the "new" meaning of local in the documentation. That is, for events that can trigger at pre-defined locations (think _compile-time_), returning `DISABLE` will do the current job, otherwise it is ignored. For example, `PY_START` is a local event with instrumentation at a guaranteed single location. Returning `DISABLE` from its handler would undo the instrumentation, which is effectively equivalent to turning the event off on the code object. So we already have a local event in its own category.

> If we are breaking the distinction between "local" meaning specific to a location and can be disabled, and "local" meaning can be turned on or off per code object, then we might as well make all events "local" in the second sense.

Ideally I would like the idea of having all the events local on a per-code object basis. I haven't looked at the other events, but the `PY_UNWIND` one was easy enough to implement at potentially no performance cost. If it is equally convenient to turn the other currently non-local events into local ones in this new sense then I think it would be great.

@markshannon for the sake of making progress here, would it be acceptable to merge the proposed change that makes `PY_UNWIND` "local" (and ignores `DISABLE`), and follow that up with potentially a more comprehensive change that makes all other events local in this new sense, and restrict the relevance of `DISABLE` to only some of the events? As I mentioned in my previous comment, the `PY_START` event has a similar behaviour. The fact that it can be disabled but not turned off is just a mere consequence of the implementation (which I think is hacky anyway, as shown by the "funny" coding required to handle that case in #142136), since the instrumentation for that event takes place in just a single place, regardless of the bytecode content.

Not sure if this is the best place to discuss the name, but I'm not sure if "tracing" is the best new name for `cProfile`.

First of all, I think it's a great idea to organize all of our profilers and make it a new place to host other kinds of profilers, but "tracing" actually has its own meaning (as far as I understand).

The more accurate concept against "sampling" is probably "deterministic" (and I know it's long and difficult to spell), which means we record at all function entries and exits.

"tracing" on the other hand, often implies that we have not only the accumulated data for function calls, but also the information of *each* call - so that we can visualize it on a timeline. If you google tracing profiler, `Perfetto` might be one of the tools that catch your eyes - that's a real tracing tool (or chrome tracing which is its predecessor). [VizTracer](https://github.com/gaogaotiantian/viztracer) is a tracing profiler for Python. It generates a tracing graph, which looks like a flamegraph but it's not.

`cProfile` does not have the capability. It can only accumulate data and summarize it. Calling it a tracing profiler might confuse people (and might take the position of an actual tracing profiler we want to add in the future).

From another perpective, `cProfile` does not use `sys.settrace`, which is another "trace" concept that exists in CPython already.

Do you think we should come up with another name for `cProfile` in the new package?

```python
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

class GenericClass(Generic[BaseClassType]):
    def a_method(self) -> BaseClassType:
        pass


class ConcreteClass(GenericClass["ConcreteFriendClass"]):
    pass


GenericClassType = TypeVar("GenericClassType", bound=GenericClass)


class GenericFriendClass(Generic[GenericClassType]):
    def a_method(self) -> GenericClassType:
        pass
```

It seems there are two related bugs in the encoder (introduced in gh-95382):

1. Uninitialized cache access: When `c_make_encoder` is called with `_current_indent_level > 0`, the cache is created with only 1 element, but `update_indent_cache` expects the cache to be incrementally built starting from level 0. This causes out-of-bounds memory access.
2.  Re-entrant `__mul__` vulnerability:` PySequence_Repeat(s->indent, indent_level)` in `create_indent_cache` can execute arbitrary Python code through a custom `__mul__` method, potentially causing use-after-free.


I have a little branch with a potential solution:  two validation checks in `_json.c`:

1. Type check in `encoder_new`: Require indent to be str or None (reject non-string objects like integers or lists that would fail later anyway).
2. Indent level check in encoder_call: Require `_current_indent_level == 0` when indent is set. This:
  - Prevents the uninitialized cache access (the cache is designed to start at level 0)
  - Eliminates the `__mul__` attack vector since PySequence_Repeat is only called when `indent_level != 0`

I think it might also be useful in a few cases for choosing reasonable defaults: i.e., does a thread-pool or multiprocessing backend make more sense as a default in some library (like PyTorch data loaders or joblib).

There seem to be some mistunderstandings here, so I would like to clarify that:

- Fixing a vulnerability has to break backwards compatibility with regard to the vulnerability. That's expected and a feature, not a bug.

- TLS is not just for privacy — not just for passwords and bank account information —, but also crucial for _authenticity_ of the data. The only scenario where a non-TLS data connection is reasonable is where the application driving the FTP transfer *verifies all received data* after retrieval; e.g. Debian verifies package files downloaded through a potentially non-TLS connection by checking GnuPG signatures. That already means zero calls like directory listings through the data channel where the client has no way of verifying that information. In the case of the application doing post-download verification, `ftplib.FTP_TLS` can be told via `.prot_c()` that the application does verification, and will do zero unverifiable calls for metadata like directory listings. Use cases "servers sending file lists", "pre-encrypted data" and "non-sensitive data" or "anonymous FTP" all forget about *authenticity*.

- The operator of the FTP server and of the FTP client are not guaranteed to be the same party, so FTP client security cannot depend on secure FTP server connection. The client is fully responsible for their own security, and so is `ftplib.FTP_TLS`.

- Documenting vulnerabilities is not fixing vulnerabilities, not reading (or overlooking) documentation does not make a user deserve exploitation, and defaults need to be secure, not documented insecure.

> Fixing a vulnerability has to break backwards compatibility with regard to the vulnerability. That's expected and a feature, not a bug.

As said previously, such major change requires a PEP to explain the rationale and provide a way to opt-out to get the old ("unsafe") behavior.

For anyone coming here looking for how to do this with `asyncio` currently, here's an implementation I came up with. It might not work 100% of the time and may have unintended consequences, but in most cases it seems to work as expected:

```python
import asyncio
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager


@asynccontextmanager
async def cancel_shield():
    task = asyncio.current_task()
    cancel_messages: list[str | None] = []
    task.cancel = lambda msg: cancel_messages.append(msg)
    task.uncancel = lambda: cancel_messages.pop()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        del task.cancel
        del task.uncancel
        for msg in cancel_messages:
            task.cancel(msg)
```

Example usage:

```python
async def work():
    async with cancel_shield():
        await asyncio.sleep(5)
        print("work done")


async def main():
    task = asyncio.create_task(work())
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    task.cancel()
    await task


asyncio.run(main())
```

I've managed to reproduce the bug on Linux for all three implementations, although note that forkserver fails in a different way from the others (potentially returns an incorrect error code rather than the process seeming alive).

Fixing it is a little tricky for the fork/spawn implementations as we don't want blocking calls to block non-blocking calls, so can't just naively take a lock and hold it across the operating system call. Hopefully my fix handles everything correctly: it is still possible for a non-blocking call racing with a blocking one to "incorrectly" return indicating the process is alive, however as the process could die at any time calling code should already be prepared to handle this.

Note that the implementations rely on `multiprocessing.connection.wait` to determine whether a call to `poll` would block.  I have checked this and believe it should be thread-safe: the call will never block after `wait` says it is ready no matter what other threads do in the interim, although it may return an error instead of the exit code for threads losing the race. However if that is mistaken we could potentially have "non-blocking" calls hanging indefinitely: if possible someone with more experience with the multiprocessing code should double-check that.

```python
MAX_ITERATIONS=10

original_excepthook = threading.excepthook

threading.excepthook = on_except

def runner(barrier):

def waiter(barrier, proc):
    barrier.wait()
    proc.join()
    assert not proc.is_alive()
    assert proc.exitcode == 0

if __name__ == '__main__':

        threads = [threading.Thread(target=waiter, args=(barrier, proc)) for _ in range(THREAD_COUNT)]
        for t in threads:

        proc.start()
        for t in threads:
```

```
[..]
NumPy may be doing some worse than typical stuff here, but right now it seems to me that Python should be protecting us.
```

`clear_memo()` is incompatible with the MEMOIZE opcode. It works with PUT, BINPUT and LONG_BINPUT, i.e. with protocol <= 3. I do not have good solution for this. Possible solutions:

* Disabling MEMOIZE after clearing the memo.
* Track the next memo index and do not reset it by `clear_memo()`.

This will lead to a silent degradation of pickle size and performance, but at least the result can be correctly unpickled.

We can also introduce an opcode for clearing the memo in the loader, but this is a PEP-level change. I am not sure that we have enough of good use cases for such feature.

cc @pitrou

We can also combine two solutions -- disable MEMOIZE until the memo size achieve its maximal size before clearing. After that, MEMOIZE can be used. It still has impact.

Alternatively, we can deprecate `clear_memo()`. The user can just create a new `Pickler` instance with the same output file.

If creating a new `Pickler` instance for every portion of data is too costly, we should add also `clear_memo()` in `Unpickler`, to avoid creating multiple `Unpickler` instances on the receiving end.

In any case this is a difficult-to-use-correctly feature.

Returning to the original issue. When pickling fails, it not only leave not pickled objects in memo. It leave also partial pickle data in the output stream. You should not just ignore error and continue pickling to the same stream, because you will not be able to load data back if some of pickles are broken. In your example you get an empty stream only because the pickled data is cached in the C implementation. But in the Python implementation you will get unfinished pickle, as well as when pickle larger data. This is an implementation detail, don't rely on it.

You can save position in the stream and restore it after pickling error. If you do this, you should also save the copy of the memo and restore it after error.

```py
saved_pos = f.tell()
saved_memo = pickler.memo.copy()
try:
    pickler.dump(bad_data)
except (PicklingError, TypeError, ...):
    f.seek(saved_pos)
    pickler.memo = saved_memo

pickler.dump(good_data)
```

About the use of `clear_memo()`. If you use it during pickling, you should also clear memo during unpickling. There is no `Unpickler.clear_memo()`, but you can use `memo.clear()` or `memo = {}`.

```py
pickler.dump(data1)
pickler.clear_memo()  # or pickler.memo.clear(), or pickler.memo = {}
pickler.dump(data2)
pickler.dump(data3)
...
data1 = unpickler.load()
umpickler.memo.clear()  # or unpickler.memo = {}
data2 = unpickler.load()
data3 = unpickler.load()
```

You can also not simply clear, but save and restore the memo.

```py
pickler.dump(data1)
saved_memo = pickler.memo.copy()
pickler.dump(data2)  # share objects with data1
pickler.memo = saved_memo
pickler.dump(data3)  # share objects with data1, but not with data2
...
data1 = unpickler.load()
saved_memo = unpickler.memo.copy()
data2 = unpickler.load()  # share objects with data1
unpickler.memo = saved_memo
data3 = unpickler.load()  # share objects with data1, but not with data2
```

Or share the memo between different picklers:
```py
pickler1.dump(data1)
pickler2.memo = pickler1.memo
pickler2.dump(data2)
...
data1 = unpickler1.load()
unpickler2.memo = unpickler1.memo
data2 = unpickler2.load()
```

I think `assertNotRaises` is worth reconsidering as its usefulness goes beyond distinguishing failures from errors (which admittedly doesn't matter much in practice). What is more important to me is that when used with the `msg` parameter, it allows adding more context to the assertion failure, especially in tests with multiple assertions.

Consider testing the validation logic of a Django model, e.g. a custom [`clean()`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/ref/models/instances/#django.db.models.Model.clean) method. Django expects `clean()` to raise a `ValidationError` if the model instance is invalid, as in the following example:

```python
from django.db import models


class Vacation(models.Model):
    start = models.DateField()
    end = models.DateField()

    def clean(self):
        if self.start > self.end:
            raise ValueError("End date must be after start date.")
```

Using `assertRaises`, testing invalid states with a meaningful failure message is straightforward:

```python
with self.assertRaises(ValidationError, msg="End date before start date should be rejected"):
    start = date(2026, 1, 11)
    end = date(206, 1, 10)
    Vacation(start=start, end=end).clean()
```

But what about asserting that a particular edge case is valid (such as the start and end date being equal in the example above)? Sure, I could just do this:

```python
start = end = date(2026, 1, 11)
Vacation(start=start, end=end).clean()  # should not raise
```

But then when a `ValidationError` is unexpectedly raised, the test output only shows the error and stack trace without any context. One could work around this by catching the error and using `self.fail()`, like this:

```python
try:
    start = end = date(2026, 1, 11)
    Vacation(start=start, end=end).clean()
except ValidationError:
    self.fail("Start and equal to end date was not accepted")
```

But then I lose the error stack trace, which may be useful to debug the issue.

`assertNotRaises` with `msg`, on the other hand, would give me both context *and* a stack trace:


```python
with self.assertNotRaises(ValidationError, msg="Start date equal to end date should be allowed"):
	start = end = date(2026, 1, 11)
	Vacation(start=start, end=end).clean() 
```

Malicious `__setitem__` is out of table. If you execute malicious code, a crash is the smallest of your problems. More plausible scenario is concurrent calls of `Unpickler.load()` in different threads or in the garbage collector. `Unpickler.load()` is not designed for reentrancy, it would not work correctly even without a crash.

The simplest solution would be to add a flag and forbid re-entering `Unpickler.load()`, `Pickler.dump()`, etc. I am not sure it is worth to do for Python implementation.

```py
partial(func, Placeholder, *args)
```
Currently, if `args` is variable, we are forced to write:
```py

```
Allowing trailing Placeholders will remove an artificial special case.

> partial(func, Placeholder, *args) if args else func

Or even worse if there is a need for type consistency:
```python
partial(func, Placeholder, *args) if args else partial(func)
```

To me it feels a bit counter-intuitive that:
```python
partial(func)                 # Ok
partial(func, Placeholder)    # Not ok
partial(func, Placeholder, 1) # Ok again
```

> Also "There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it."
> 
> With a trailing `Placeholder`, it's no different than just using `partial` as-is, other than the positional-only requirement.

I don't think this Zen part is strongly applicable here and I think principles of orthogonality and modularity have a bigger weight here.

This case, to me, seems more like forbidding empty `it` for `[*it]`, because there should be only one way to do it and we already have `[]`.

> Speaking of which, I'd like to hear more about this use-case. If something is supposed to be positional-only, then generally that would be done at the function-level, not in `partial`.

Well this is kind of the thing of `partial` - it transforms the argument spec. It is the same as saying: "if different default is needed, then it should have been set in underlying function in the first place".

I think removing this prohibition smooths out the interface making it more intuitive (as per my post above):
1. `partial` accepts `Placeholder`, which transforms argument into `positional only`
2. Thus, if I write `partial(func, Placeholder)`, the result is as expected - no ambiguity here.

Exact same reasoning has already been used (consciously or not):
1. `partial` substitutes new arguments into `func`
2. Thus, if I write `partial(func)` without any substitutions, I get `partial`, which has the same `argspec` as underlying `func`

There are other POVs from which this can be argued, but I think they can be neutralised by simple "consenting adults" as implications are rather trivial. For the sake of intuitive API and smooth programatic usage.

Correction: Python does neither verify certificate nor hostname for SMTP, IMAP, and so on. Applications are subject to man-in-the-middle attacks for these protocols unless they pass an explicit context.

```
>>> import ssl
>>> ctx = ssl._create_stdlib_context()
>>> ctx.verify_mode
<VerifyMode.CERT_NONE: 0>
>>> ctx.check_hostname
False
```

The recommended workaround is:

```
import ssl

ssl._create_stdlib_context = ssl.create_default_context
```

or

```
import ssl

def verified_stdlib_context(protocol=None, *, cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_REQUIRED, check_hostname=True, **kwargs):
    return ssl._create_unverified_context(protocol, cert_reqs=cert_reqs, check_hostname=check_hostname, **kwargs)

ssl._create_stdlib_context = verified_stdlib_context
```

This enables cert validation and hostname verification for all stdlib modules.

> Let me try to give you the Odoo point of view, for the sake of adding
> context to the Python proposal.
> 
> For us, this change would not only be backwards-incompatible, but also
> quite risky. If it became the default, we may even need to change it back
> to *opt-in*.
> As you can imagine, our users configure all kinds of outgoing mail servers,
> in various contexts (prod, staging, test). The SMTP landscape is incredibly
> messy, and many small businesses still rely on custom SMTP deployments or
> low-quality third-party ones. Maintaining a valid TLS certificate chain is
> quite difficult, especially nowadays with short-lived certs.
> So activating the TLS verification is guaranteed to break a good number of
> real life deployments, and not just the test ones.
> 
> You could say that forcing users to notice the problem and upgrade their
> setup is good, so we could make this the default in the next Odoo version.
> But the reality may be more *nuanced*.
> Some users may enable STARTTLS to follow recommendations, but don't have
> the resources or skills to maintain a valid cert. Not only does it require
> a frequently-updated TLS cert, it also requires the cert to match the
> server hostname. This is not as trivial as it seems in the world of virtual
> hosting, where hosting providers offer aliases for custom domains (e.g.
> smtp.mydomain.org), but serve a generic TLS cert on it (ssl0.ovh.net).
> Many users are more likely to abandon TLS and switch to plaintext, if it
> turns out to be too complicated to set up and maintain.
> 
> Now you may say that they'd be better off using plaintext than experiencing
> a false sense of security. That's not really true in practice, it's
> still a *net loss* in terms of security: their SMTP credentials would now be exposed in
> plaintext, along with all their communications. And it does not require a
> MITM attacker, a simple packet dump on unencrypted free wifi is enough to
> capture that.
> This is generally true for all TLS channels, including HTTPS: having *an
> invalid certificate is still better than cleartext communication*.
> 
> Browsers usually solve this problem by allowing users to *bypass the
> verification process interactively* if they know what they are doing.
> Unfortunately Odoo users aren't generally in control of the SMTP parameters
> when they're using the system, so they wouldn't be allowed to make an
> exception dynamically. Blocking their messages because the TLS certificate
> has just expired would simply cause a *denial of service, with no graceful
> degradation*.
> 
> So if we want to enable TLS verification, I suspect we'll either have to
> make it opt-in, or to implement some automatic detection with an easy
> exception mechanism, during setup.
> I have created a *backlog task* to discuss it internally (task-2861790).
>
> Odoo's case is perhaps unusual though, due to a large proportion of legacy,
mixed deployment environments ;-)

This is the patch created by Claude Code:

```C
diff --git a/Python/ast_preprocess.c b/Python/ast_preprocess.c
index d45435257cc..a1a32068a67 100644
--- a/Python/ast_preprocess.c
+++ b/Python/ast_preprocess.c
@@ -581,6 +581,81 @@ astfold_expr(expr_ty node_, PyArena *ctx_, _PyASTPreprocessState *state)
         CALL(astfold_expr, expr_ty, node_->v.Call.func);
         CALL_SEQ(astfold_expr, expr, node_->v.Call.args);
         CALL_SEQ(astfold_keyword, keyword, node_->v.Call.keywords);
+
+        // Optimize tuple(genexpr) -> tuple([listcomp])
+        // This eliminates generator object creation overhead
+        if (node_->v.Call.func->kind == Name_kind &&
+            asdl_seq_LEN(node_->v.Call.args) == 1 &&
+            asdl_seq_LEN(node_->v.Call.keywords) == 0) {
+
+            expr_ty arg = asdl_seq_GET(node_->v.Call.args, 0);
+            PyObject *name = node_->v.Call.func->v.Name.id;
+
+            // Transform tuple(genexpr) to tuple([listcomp])
+            if (_PyUnicode_EqualToASCIIString(name, "tuple") &&
+                arg->kind == GeneratorExp_kind) {
+                expr_ty listcomp = _PyAST_ListComp(
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.elt,
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.generators,
+                    arg->lineno, arg->col_offset,
+                    arg->end_lineno, arg->end_col_offset, ctx_);
+                if (listcomp == NULL) {
+                    return 0;
+                }
+                asdl_seq_SET(node_->v.Call.args, 0, listcomp);
+            }
+            // Transform list(genexpr) to [listcomp]
+            else if (_PyUnicode_EqualToASCIIString(name, "list") &&
+                     arg->kind == GeneratorExp_kind) {
+                expr_ty listcomp = _PyAST_ListComp(
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.elt,
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.generators,
+                    arg->lineno, arg->col_offset,
+                    arg->end_lineno, arg->end_col_offset, ctx_);
+                if (listcomp == NULL) {
+                    return 0;
+                }
+                // Replace the entire Call node with just the listcomp
+                *node_ = *listcomp;
+            }
+            // Transform set(genexpr) to {setcomp}
+            else if (_PyUnicode_EqualToASCIIString(name, "set") &&
+                     arg->kind == GeneratorExp_kind) {
+                expr_ty setcomp = _PyAST_SetComp(
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.elt,
+                    arg->v.GeneratorExp.generators,
+                    arg->lineno, arg->col_offset,
+                    arg->end_lineno, arg->end_col_offset, ctx_);
+                if (setcomp == NULL) {
+                    return 0;
+                }
+                // Replace the entire Call node with just the setcomp
+                *node_ = *setcomp;
+            }
+            // Transform dict((k, v) for ...) to {k: v for ...}
+            else if (_PyUnicode_EqualToASCIIString(name, "dict") &&
+                     arg->kind == GeneratorExp_kind) {
+                // Check if the genexpr yields tuples with exactly 2 elements
+                expr_ty elt = arg->v.GeneratorExp.elt;
+                if (elt->kind == Tuple_kind &&
+                    asdl_seq_LEN(elt->v.Tuple.elts) == 2) {
+                    // Extract key and value from the tuple
+                    expr_ty key = asdl_seq_GET(elt->v.Tuple.elts, 0);
+                    expr_ty value = asdl_seq_GET(elt->v.Tuple.elts, 1);
+
+                    expr_ty dictcomp = _PyAST_DictComp(
+                        key, value,
+                        arg->v.GeneratorExp.generators,
+                        arg->lineno, arg->col_offset,
+                        arg->end_lineno, arg->end_col_offset, ctx_);
+                    if (dictcomp == NULL) {
+                        return 0;
+                    }
+                    // Replace the entire Call node with just the dictcomp
+                    *node_ = *dictcomp;
+                }
+            }
+        }
         break;
     case FormattedValue_kind:
         CALL(astfold_expr, expr_ty, node_->v.FormattedValue.value);
```

This is a well-motivated feature request. The use case for querying the wakeup fd without side effects is clear, especially for nested signal handling contexts.

## Implementation Approach

The C-level implementation would be straightforward in `Modules/signalmodule.c`:

```c
static PyObject *
signal_get_wakeup_fd(PyObject *self, PyObject *Py_UNUSED(ignored))
{
    return PyLong_FromLong(wakeup.fd);
}
```

This avoids both problems you mentioned:
1. No race condition between two `set_wakeup_fd()` calls
2. Preserves the `warn_on_full_buffer` state

## API Considerations

Should `get_wakeup_fd()` also return the `warn_on_full_buffer` state? Options:

**Option 1**: Just return fd (simple)
```python
fd = signal.get_wakeup_fd()  # returns int
```

**Option 2**: Return tuple with both values (more complete)
```python
fd, warn_on_full = signal.get_wakeup_fd()  # returns (int, bool)
```

Option 2 would be more symmetric with `set_wakeup_fd(fd, *, warn_on_full_buffer=True)` and allow full state inspection, but breaks the simple int return type convention.

## Thread Safety

Since `wakeup.fd` is only modified/read in the main thread (enforced by `set_wakeup_fd`), the getter would have the same thread safety guarantees as the setter.

In my opinion, this only hides the lack of an explicit save-restore mechanism. Suppose we have `get_wakeup_token()`, `save_wakeup_token()`, and `restore_wakeup_token()`. Then we could suggest the following behavior:

1. `token = get_wakeup_token()` returns the current information (in the form of token attributes): `fd`, `warn_on_full_buffer`, possibly `is_socket`.
2. `outer_token = save_wakeup_token(maybe_token)` returns the current information and replaces it with the passed one. If the token was not passed (is `None`?), `fd=-1` is implied.
3. `inner_token = restore_wakeup_token(outer_token)` also returns the current information and replaces it with the passed one, but the token is not optional. Both functions can be expressed as one (as `set_wakeup_token()`/`reset_wakeup_token()`), but separating them makes things clearer and prevents errors.

This allows to notify about signals using different strategies (add a switch function?):

1. Send signal numbers via the current token's fd. Corresponds to the current behavior. The simplest way to wake up the main thread, but not suitable for guests (since they will not be woken up and therefore will not be able to execute their signal handlers registered by the event loop).
2. Send signal numbers via the fd of the "deepest" token. The information will have to be stored as a list of lists or a tree (perhaps storing child tokens as an attribute of the parent?). Notification will be done by walking the tree, where only the fds of tokens that have no children (or have `warn_on_full_buffer=True`) will be notified. A relatively expensive method, but it allows all guests to be woken up (all guests will be able to execute their signal handlers).

The second strategy is currently impossible to implement without using a wakeup pair, an additional thread, and monkey patching (to track the current wakeup fd). And unlike the approach I described in this issue, it allows to completely isolate the wakeup fd (the host will know nothing about the guests).

I would like to add some explanations about my approach with conditional setting. If the host does not set the wakeup fd, the main thread may not wake up when a signal arrives and thus may not execute signal handlers (there are several very old issues about this). Therefore, the guest spreads its wakeup fd to the host level while this is the case, thereby waking up the host (the main thread) when a signal arrives. Otherwise, this is not required, and the wakeup fds are isolated from each other (not least to prevent conflicts between guests of the same depth level).

The approach solves the problem of waking up the main thread, but not the problem of waking up the guest. Signal handlers registered by the guest's event loop will only be executed if the host does not use `set_wakeup_fd()`. This may be sufficient in most cases, but it is still a limitation.

I think the whole concept of slots (the `tp_...` slots, not `__slots__` or `PyType_Slot`) as an optimization is the root of the problem, they slow down class creation and don't help performance as they complicate the real optimizations that we perform.

We should view the `tp_slots` as doing two distinct things: 
1. Specifying the behavior of operations when the `struct _typeobject` is passed to `PyType_Ready` 
2. A backwards compatible way for C extensions to access operations. Eg. `iter(i)` as `Py_TYPE(i)->tp_iter`

For pure Python objects, all slots can be filled in with a function that does the dynamic lookup, which should be very quick.
Once resolved, we can overwrite the slot with a more direct version.

For classes defined by `struct _typeobject` we can just replace the `NULL`s with the dynamic lookup function.
For classes defined from `PyType_Spec` we fill in the defined slots and then replace the `NULL`s with the dynamic lookup function.


@serhiy-storchaka The proposed `python -m module:function` syntax has a key advantage over `python -m module function` - it mirrors the standard entry-point spec syntax that devs already know from `pyproject.toml`.

## Implementation Notes

This would need changes in `runpy._run_module_as_main()`. The parsing is straightforward:

```python
if ':' in mod_name and not mod_name.endswith(':'):
    module_name, attr_name = mod_name.rsplit(':', 1)
    # Load module, get attribute, call it
else:
    # Existing behavior
```

## Compatibility Considerations

The `:` character is already invalid in Python module names (would cause `SyntaxError`), so there's zero risk of breaking existing `-m` usage. This is purely additive.

## argv Behavior

Should match console_scripts semantics:
- `argv[0]` = entry point ref (e.g., `"module:func"` or just the script name)  
- `argv[1:]` = passed args

This maintains consistency with how installed entry points work today.

The reproducer is counter intuitive, at the first look, `with my_wrapped_open():` seems to close the `TextIOWrapper` when Python exits the block. But nope, it calls `my_wrapped_open()` exit handler.

Here is the fixed example, using `with fp:` block:

```py
import io
import tempfile
import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def my_wrapped_open():
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('bw') as handle:
        handle.write(b'content')
        handle.seek(0)
        yield io.TextIOWrapper(handle, encoding='utf-8')

with my_wrapped_open() as fp:
    with fp:
        pass
```

The `with fp:` statement makes sure that `io.TextIOWrapper.close()` is closed when Python exits this block.

---

Another example to explain the issue:

```py
import io
import contextlib

class Open:
    def __init__(self):
        self.closed = False

    def __enter__(self):
        pass

    def __exit__(self, *args):
        print("Open.__exit__: close")
        self.closed = True

    def __del__(self, print=print):
        if self.closed:
            return
        print("Warning: %r was not closed" % self)

@contextlib.contextmanager
def my_wrapped_open():
    yield Open()

with my_wrapped_open() as fp:
    with fp:
        print("exit 'with fp:'")
    print("exit 'with my_wrapped_open() as fp:'")
print("exit")
```

Output:

```
exit 'with fp:'
Open.__exit__: close
exit 'with my_wrapped_open() as fp:'
exit
```

Output without `with fp:` block:

```
exit 'with my_wrapped_open() as fp:'
exit
Warning: <__main__.Open object at 0x7fe577669d30> was not closed
```

The non-ASCII decimal digits have some backing in Unicode -- there are official categories for decimal digits, and their values. [1]

Adding a character after of seeing it used in a table is a bad precedent; it leaves us with *unbounded scope* for similar requests in the future. That's not a good thing to maintain.

I've decided to increase the number of levels to the following:

- **incompatible**: Not safe even with external locking
- **compatible**: Safe if the caller serializes all access with external locks
- **distinct**: Safe to call without external synchronization on distinct objects
- **shared**: Safe to call without external synchronization on the same shared object
- **atomic**: Appears atomic to all threads

Both `Struct.__new__` and `Struct.__init__` can be called explicitly (in the overwritten `__new__` or `__init__`) or implicitly (when `__new__` or `__init__` are not defined in a Struct subclass). We can check `tp_new` and `tp_init` of the current class. If they are the same as in the base class, they were called implicitly. I believe I've run into a pathological case of this in the real world. A tight loop happening at just the right call depth lead to an explosion of mmap/munmap calls when upgarding from Python 3.12 to 3.14 (12x the number of allocs/deallocs), because the size of the frame changed by one pointer. Here's a reproducer Claude Code came up with:

```python
import sys

BRANCHES = 1000  # Number of sibling calls at the critical depth

def level(d):
    """Recurse to fill the 16KB chunk, then fan out."""
    # 20 locals to make each frame ~35-36 words (FRAME_SPECIALS_SIZE + locals + stack)
    _a=_b=_c=_d=_e=_f=_g=_h=_i=_j=None
    _k=_l=_m=_n=_o=_p=_q=_r=_s=_t=None
    if d > 0:
        level(d - 1)
    else:
        # At the critical depth, each burner() call crosses the chunk boundary,
        # triggering mmap+munmap. Without chunk caching, this is O(BRANCHES)
        # kernel calls instead of O(1).
        for _ in range(BRANCHES):
            burner()

def burner():
    """Leaf function that crosses the chunk boundary."""
    _a=_b=_c=_d=_e=_f=_g=_h=_i=_j=None
    _k=_l=_m=_n=_o=_p=_q=_r=_s=_t=None
    return None

def _framesize(code):
    """Estimate frame size in words (FRAME_SPECIALS_SIZE + locals + stack)."""
    specials = 10 if sys.version_info >= (3, 13) else 9
    return (specials + code.co_nlocals
            + len(code.co_cellvars) + len(code.co_freevars)
            + code.co_stacksize)

def find_thrash_depth():
    """Auto-calibrate: find the depth where burner() just crosses the boundary.

    The 16KB root chunk holds ~2044 usable words. We compute frame sizes for
    level(), burner(), and the module code to find the exact depth where the
    chunk fills to within burner_sz of the top.

    Returns (depth, level_sz, burner_sz, base).
    """
    try:
        import _testinternalcapi
        level_sz = _testinternalcapi.get_co_framesize(level.__code__)
        burner_sz = _testinternalcapi.get_co_framesize(burner.__code__)
        base = _testinternalcapi.get_co_framesize(sys._getframe(1).f_code)
    except (ImportError, AttributeError):
        level_sz = _framesize(level.__code__)
        burner_sz = _framesize(burner.__code__)
        base = _framesize(sys._getframe(1).f_code)

    usable = 2044  # words in root chunk

    for d in range(40, 80):
        remaining = usable - base - (d + 1) * level_sz
        if 0 < remaining < burner_sz:
            return d, level_sz, burner_sz, base

    return None, level_sz, burner_sz, base

if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    depth = int(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"Python {sys.version.split()[0]} | depth={depth} | branches={BRANCHES}")
else:
    result, level_sz, burner_sz, base = find_thrash_depth()
    if result is not None:
        depth = result
        print(f"Python {sys.version.split()[0]} | depth={depth} | branches={BRANCHES}"
              f" | level_sz={level_sz} burner_sz={burner_sz} base={base}")
    else:
        # No thrashing depth: level_sz > burner_sz and alignment skips the window.
        # Fall back to depth 55 for comparison.
        depth = 55
        print(f"Python {sys.version.split()[0]} | depth={depth} (fallback) | branches={BRANCHES}"
              f" | level_sz={level_sz} burner_sz={burner_sz} base={base}")
        print(f"  No thrashing depth found for this build.")

print(f"Run with: strace -e mmap,munmap -c python3 {__file__}")
level(depth)
print("Done.")
```

In other words I don't think you people need to be running `ldconfig` and reading its output at all, let the dynamic linker do the discovery instead. The dynamic linker will check a lot more locations than what `ldconfig` looks at, like: 

* `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`

* `--library-path` (yes you can run the dynamic linker directly)

* the rpath in the binaries/libraries, this includes relative paths like `$ORIGIN/../../lib` where `$ORIGIN` is the location of the library/binary.

https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html ``` If a shared object dependency does not contain a slash, then it is searched for in the following order: (1) Using the directories specified in the DT_RPATH dynamic section attribute of the binary if present and DT_RUNPATH attribute does not exist. (2) Using the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH, unless the executable is being run in secure-execution mode (see below), in which case this variable is ignored. (3) Using the directories specified in the DT_RUNPATH dynamic section attribute of the binary if present. Such directories are searched only to find those objects required by DT_NEEDED (direct dependencies) entries and do not apply to those objects' children, which must themselves have their own DT_RUNPATH entries. This is unlike DT_RPATH, which is applied to searches for all children in the dependency tree. (4) From the cache file /etc/ld.so.cache, which contains a compiled list of candidate shared objects previously found in the augmented library path. If, however, the binary was linked with the -z nodefaultlib linker option, shared objects in the default paths are skipped. Shared objects installed in hardware capability directories (see below) are preferred to other shared objects. (5) In the default path /lib, and then /usr/lib. (On some 64-bit architectures, the default paths for 64-bit shared objects are /lib64, and then /usr/lib64.) AFAICT, the current implementation does it as a fallback:

```py
def _findLib_ld(name):
    # See issue #9998 for why this is needed
    expr = r'[^\(\)\s]*lib%s\.[^\(\)\s]*' % re.escape(name)
    cmd = ['ld', '-t']
    libpath = os.environ.get('LD_LIBRARY_PATH')
    if libpath:
        for d in libpath.split(':'):
            cmd.extend(['-L', d])
    cmd.extend(['-o', os.devnull, '-l%s' % name])
    result = None
    try:
        p = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                             stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
                             universal_newlines=True)
        out, _ = p.communicate()
        res = re.findall(expr, os.fsdecode(out))
        for file in res:
            # Check if the given file is an elf file: gcc can report
            # some files that are linker scripts and not actual
            # shared objects. See bpo-41976 for more details
            if not _is_elf(file):
                continue
            return os.fsdecode(file)
    except Exception:
        pass  # result will be None
    return result
```

Indeed this looks like a legitimate bug. Maybe I was too explicit about "waiting" for triaging but usually:

- Hard crashes that you can yourself reproduce without messing up with code objects themselves (that is, using `code.__replace__`) should usually be assumed to be bugs themselves. When the patch is really simple and the regression test as well, it's fine to open a PR. If the issue is much more complex or touches sensitive parts of the interpreter, it's usually better to wait for other core devs to decide how to tackle the issue (unless there's an obvious way to do it).
- Bugs in pure Python code may or may not bugs so it's better to wait for the issue to be triaged or be _really_ sure about it. However, trivial fixes such as typos in the docs can be done without an issue (only typos in user-facing docs are usually accepted as otherwise they introduce code churn). Most of the time, bugs are either issues in the documentation where it's imprecise but the behavior is expected, or real bugs where the documentation is correct but the actual code does something else. And ... sometimes it's just something that we can't change because it'd be highly backward incompatible and the ship has already sailed.
- Features usually require to wait for a discussion. Opening a PR without a discussion is a no go in general and I tend to close them because otherwise they remain open for too long.

Yes, definitely; I've been gradually helping on the docs I've/we've touched anyway, though it is a long term project. I've found a number of things that were undocumented, as well as a number of other real issues through that, e.g. on the `sqlite3` module that Erlend and I fixed.

> Most of them are innocent, like using :const: while referring to a constant defined in another file, or using :meth:`__init__` to speak about the concept of an init method.

I'd argue neither is exactly innocent:

* For the first, unless there's some particular reason not to, it usually makes sense to actually cross reference the constant, so the reader can find out more, and be explicit about it's location at least in the source (since `~` can hide that in the rendered output if not desired). This also means if the constant is renamed, moved or removed, Sphinx will issue a warning about it.
* For the second, doing `` :meth:`~object.__init__` `` to cross reference the full description of an `__init__` method will often still have value to readers, at least on first usage in a context, and doesn't take up any more space. We could _potentially_ extend the `:meth:` role to automatically prepend a default name, i.e. `object`, to `:meth:` and `:attr:` that only have a single component, and perform the lookup with that—though the Sphinx built in roles are not the best structured to be able to extend easily without copying a fair bit of code.

> For the innocent usages of rst markers, there's two fixes:

There's a third, much simpler and better fix. If the link isn't desired, every Sphinx cross-reference role supports prepending `!` to prevent Sphinx from trying to resolve the reference, which avoids both the warning and the (very slight) build-time lookup cost, while preserving both all the information in the source, and the formatting in the output (since the formatting of named roles and regular literals is not the same, at least in our current theme), while being easier than both (just add one character). So, you could just do:

`` :const:`!IGNORECASE` ``

As a general note of caution, especially when submitting PRs fixing these sorts of widespread and potentially nitpicky (heh) docs defects, especially when in cases like this there are a number of different possibilities to handle each warning instance, we should take care to avoid the folly of large "omnibus" PRs (as Guido likes to call them) and take care to consider each specific change we're making holistically, and ensure that we're picking the approach that best serves the reader in for each specific context, as opposed to just applying one type of fix mechanically to all instances, or even worse arbitrarily picking one or another each time without careful thought and consideration that might fix the warning but be an overall regression.

Otherwise, if we're too focused solely on the narrow objective of getting rid of the warnings by whatever means, as opposed to the broader goal of improving the overall quality of the docs, we risk both doing exactly the opposite of the latter, and consuming the limited time and churn budget of core developers and other reviewers on changes with little or even negative practical benefit.

> I don't remember reading about '~object' or '!CON' and I imaging others are similarly deficient in sphinx-fu.

@ezio-melotti made a [nice quick-reference table](https://devguide.python.org/documentation/markup/#quick-reference) with all of the common syntax bits, including those, over on the devguide, and the Sphinx docs also has [a concise primer](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/restructuredtext/roles.html#cross-referencing-syntax) covering those as well, but TL;DR these are the main cases:

* If the object exists and *should be formally documented* but isn't, either **document it** or **leave the warning** until it is

* If an object exists but is *unintentionally broken* due to the wrong class, module, etc. prefix, a typo, etc, **fix it**

* If an object is missing an *implicit prefix* that should not be displayed in the final output, like `object` for dunder methods or the class name when methods are listed individually, **add the prefix with a prepended a `~`** to hide it (e.g. `` :meth:`~object.__str__` ``, ``the :meth:`~Spam.get_foo` method of the :class:`Spam` class``)

* If an object was *removed from Python*, is *deliberately undocumented* or is a *subsequent reference* to something already linked in the the same scope, **prepend `!`** to not resolve the reference (e.g. `` :meth:`!Spam.removed_method` ``, `` :c:func:`!_internal_api` ``)

* If an object is *an example* or not otherwise a "real" class, function, etc., either do the above or **use a literal** (e.g. ``` ``ExampleClass.example_attr`` ``` ``` ``fake_func()`` ```).

I created PR #107298 to fix some Sphinx warnings in the C API Documentation.

For newer contributors looking to tackle this, be advised there's no one size fits all approach that's the right one for every warning; instead, there are a handful of common cases covering the great majority of them, and a few few edge/special cases for the rest.

I'd like to write up a proper mini-guide for this, but my bandwidth is limited at the moment. However, here's an overview of how to handle the most common cases. If you have something that isn't covered here, feel free to reply and suggest it be added, or if you have questions about a special case, I'm always happy to answer.

In summary, here's a basic algorithm for determining such:

1. Check the named target. If it is:
    * clearly _not_ something that should be a linkable cross reference (example object, sample code, etc), replace the ref role with literals.
    * a standard C function, system call, environment variable, etc, add it to `conf.py`.
    * a documented function with parameters specified in the ref, specify just the callable name inside `<>` after the existing text
    * A generic dunder method (e.g. `__init__`), prepend `~object.` (or a more specific class name, if present)
2. Search the target name and variations using the [Python docs search](https://docs.python.org/dev/search.html) and/or [`sphobjinv`](https://sphobjinv.readthedocs.io/en/stable/index.html). If found:
    * Determine the most appropriate target (if multiple), and fix the cross reference per **Table 1**
3. If not found in latest docs, search old versions of the docs, e.g. 5 versions back or using Google for it (see **Table 3**). If found:
    * If important to still keep in current docs, prepend the target name with `!`
    * Otherwise, remove the ref target and its relevant context
4. If seems to be a not-documented target:
    * Add/fix the reference target, per **Table 2**
5. You've found an uncovered/special case.
    * Ask here for more help.

Here's a more detailed listing of specific cases with solutions and examples, divided into a few base categories. Tables are in rough order of commonality.

## Target exists; ref doesn't correctly point to it

**Solution**: Fix the cross reference.

**Table 1**

| Case | Solution | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ref target missing class, module, etc prefix | Add missing prefix, with `~` to hide it as appropriate | `` :func:`exit` in :mod:`sys` `` -> `` :func:`~sys.exit` in :mod:`sys` `` | 
| Generic dunder method (e.g. `__init__`) missing prefix | Add missing prefix: A custom class if specifically documented under such, else `~object` | `` :meth:`__init__` `` -> `` :meth:`~object.__init__` ``|
| Missing domain prefix (`c:`, etc) | Add domain prefix | `` :func:`PyObject_Call` `` -> `` :c:func:`PyObject_Call` `` |
| Wrong role used | Use correct role | `` :class:`dataclasses.dataclass` `` -> `` :func:`dataclasses.dataclass` `` |
| Typo/mistake in target name | Fix typo/mistake | `` :func:`dataclass.dataclasses` `` -> `` :func:`dataclasses.dataclass` `` |
| API documented under other alias | Change cross-reference to "canonical" name, possibly keeping alias as displayed text | `` :meth:`turtle.RawTurtle.tiltangle` `` -> `` :func:`turtle.RawTurtle.titlangle <turtle.tiltangle>` `` |
| Documented callable with parameters | Set title to full call and target to just callable cname | `` :func:`sys.exit(0)` `` -> `` :func:`sys.exit(0) <sys.exit>` `` |


## Target doesn't exist and should

**Solution**: Add/fix the target.

**Table 2**

| Case | Solution | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API not formally documented | Properly document API | `` :func:`enum.show_flag_values` `` -> Keep plus document, e.g. `` .. function:: show_flag_values(...) `` |
| API documented under wrong directive | Fix API docs to use correct directive & update xrefs | ``:c:func:`PyObject_Call` `` with ``.. function:: PyObject_Call(...)`` -> Fix latter to `` .. c:function:: PyObject_Call(...) `` |
| API documented under wrong name | Fix API docs to use correct name; add aliases to using ref labels so fragment UIRs don't break | `` :meth:`Cursor.execute` `` with ``.. method:: Cursor.execute()`` underneath ``.. class:: Cursor`` (double class name, means target is `Cursor.Cursor.execute`) -> Fix directive to use just ``.. method:: execute()`` |


## Target doesn't exist, and used to

**Solution**: De-resolve reference if important to still keep; otherwise remove xref and relevant context.

**Table 3**

| Case | Solution | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ref target obsolete/removed | Either remove obsolete reference & associated context, or if necessary to keep, prepend `!` | `` :mod:`distutils` `` -> `` :mod:`!distutils` `` (or remove) |
| `:ref:` target label should/used to exist, but doesn't | Find where it used to/should point to, adding one if needed (or remove reference if obsolete) | `` :ref:`old-section-name` `` -> `` :ref:`new-section-name` `` (or add alias) |


## Target doesn't exist, and shouldn't

**Solution**: Remove, silence or ignore the cross reference

**Table 4**

| Case | Solution | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Example object | Use literals instead | `` :meth:`Spam.eggs` `` -> ``` ``Spam.eggs()`` ``` |
| Sample code | Use literals instead | `` :func:`print("An example use of print")` `` -> ``` ``print("An example use of print")`` ``` |
| C stdlib/system call | Add to `conf.py` ignore list | `` :c:func:`printf` `` -> Leave as-is, ignore in `conf.py` |
| Standard environment variable | Add to `conf.py` ignore list | `` :envvar:`PATH` `` -> Leave as-is, ignore in `conf.py` |

# TL;DR

When strace is gone, python process loses foreground process group. Kernel doesn't permit background process to call `tcsetattr(TCSADRAIN)`, so the underneath syscall `ioctl(fd, TCSETSW, ...)` returns `EIO`. So far it's not a big deal, but Python 3.13 new REPL handles such an error by calling `ioctl(fd, TCSETSW, ...)` again for certain reasons, leading to the infinite recursive error loop.

Set `PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1` to switch back to old REPL can avoid such an issue:
```
strace env PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1 ./python
```

# Reproduce

I can provide a easier reproducing approach without strace:

```
import os
import sys
import signal


if not sys.stdin.isatty():
    print("warning: stdin is not a TTY; REPL may not be interactive.", file=sys.stderr)

pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    exe = sys.executable
    os.execlp(exe, os.path.basename(exe))
    os._exit(127)

os.waitpid(pid, 0)
```

Run `./python child_repl.py`.

See the process tree:
```
gray       46432   30809  0 21:00 pts/0    00:00:00  |       \_ ./python child_repl.py
gray       46433   46432  0 21:00 pts/0    00:00:00  |           \_ python
```

Kill the parent python:
```
kill -9 46432
```
Send SIGINT to repl
```
kill -2 46433
```

💥 


# Details

The parent python + repl python is a foreground process group, which can legally use tty. After we kill the parent python, shell observe the group leader process exit, reclaim back the foreground process group, leaving the remaing repl python running in the background process group.

Above can be confirmed by running a script in repl:

```

...

...     pgid = os.getpgrp()
...     fg_pgid = struct.unpack("i", fcntl.ioctl(fd, termios.TIOCGPGRP, struct.pack("i", 0)))[0]
...     return pgid == fg_pgid
... 
... while 1: 
...     print("Am I foreground?", is_foreground())
...     time.sleep(1)
... 
...

Am I foreground? True

cpython $ Am I foreground? False
Am I foreground? False

```

The answer changed once the parent python got killed.

As I mentioned, kernel forbids background processes to call `tcsetattr(TCSADRAIN)`, so the following syscall for sure failed:
```
20:18:26 ioctl(3, TCGETS, {c_iflag=IXON|IUTF8, c_oflag=NL0|CR0|TAB0|BS0|VT0|FF0|OPOST|ONLCR, c_cflag=B38400|CS8|CREAD, c_lflag=ISIG|ECHOE|ECHOK|IEXTEN|ECHOCTL|ECHOKE, ...}) = 0 <0.000008> 20:18:26 ioctl(3, TCGETS, {c_iflag=IXON|IUTF8, c_oflag=NL0|CR0|TAB0|BS0|VT0|FF0|OPOST|ONLCR, c_cflag=B38400|CS8|CREAD, c_lflag=ISIG|ECHOE|ECHOK|IEXTEN|ECHOCTL|ECHOKE, ...}) = 0 <0.000006> 20:18:26 ioctl(3, TCSETSW, {c_iflag=ICRNL|IXON|IUTF8, c_oflag=NL0|CR0|TAB0|BS0|VT0|FF0|OPOST|ONLCR, c_cflag=B38400|CS8|CREAD, c_lflag=ISIG|ICANON|ECHO|ECHOE|ECHOK|IEXTEN|ECHOCTL|ECHOKE, ...}) = -1 EIO (Input/output error) <0.000007>
```

The old python repl tolerates above error, while the new repl prefers to raise the error with nice python stack. The intention was good, but the execution was bad. To print the backtrace, omehow python needs to call ioctl again, ends up with the exactly same error from kernel. That's why we see:
```
During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
```

## 6. `is_current_pgrp_orphaned`

The source code is in [exit.c](https://github.com/gregkh/linux/blob/4c1a2d4cd9a5b6c55739a80c5b9efbca322adad7/kernel/exit.c#L345):

```C
 318   │ /*
 319   │  * Determine if a process group is "orphaned", according to the POSIX
 320   │  * definition in 2.2.2.52.  Orphaned process groups are not to be affected
 321   │  * by terminal-generated stop signals.  Newly orphaned process groups are
 322   │  * to receive a SIGHUP and a SIGCONT.
 323   │  *
 324   │  * "I ask you, have you ever known what it is to be an orphan?"
 325   │  */
 326   │ static int will_become_orphaned_pgrp(struct pid *pgrp,
 327   │                                         struct task_struct *ignored_task)
 328   │ {
 329   │         struct task_struct *p;
 330   │
 331   │         do_each_pid_task(pgrp, PIDTYPE_PGID, p) {
 332   │                 if ((p == ignored_task) ||
 333   │                     (p->exit_state && thread_group_empty(p)) ||
 334   │                     is_global_init(p->real_parent))
 335   │                         continue;
 336   │
 337   │                 if (task_pgrp(p->real_parent) != pgrp &&
 338   │                     task_session(p->real_parent) == task_session(p))
 339   │                         return 0;
 340   │         } while_each_pid_task(pgrp, PIDTYPE_PGID, p);
 341   │
 342   │         return 1;
 343   │ }
 344   │
 345   │ int is_current_pgrp_orphaned(void)
 346   │ {
 347   │         int retval;
 348   │
 349   │         read_lock(&tasklist_lock);
 350   │         retval = will_become_orphaned_pgrp(task_pgrp(current), NULL);
 351   │         read_unlock(&tasklist_lock);
 352   │
 353   │         return retval;
 354   │ }
```

The comment in `will_become_orphaned_pgrp()` explains the POSIX semantics:
Orphaned process groups aren’t affected by terminal-generated stop signals. Newly orphaned groups get `SIGHUP` and `SIGCONT`.

## 7. Conclusion

The parent process group of the current process was **orphaned**.

That’s why the `ioctl` syscall fails with **-5 (`EIO`)**.

## Fix Approach

The solution is straightforward - make `BIG_TEXT` generation deterministic by sorting glob results:

```python
for fname in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(glob.escape(os.path.dirname(__file__)), '*.py'))):
    with open(fname, 'rb') as fh:
        test_size += fh.readinto(memoryview(BIG_TEXT)[test_size:])
    if test_size > 128 * 1024:
        break
```

This ensures consistent test data across all platforms and runs, eliminating the flakiness.

##Alternative: Fixed Test Data

If we want even more robustness, could generate a deterministic byte pattern instead of reading actual files:

```python
# Deterministic, compressible test data
BIG_TEXT = bytes(range(256)) * (128 * 1024 // 256)
```

But the sorted glob approach is simpler and maintains the current test philosophy of using "real" Python code as test data.

Happy to submit a PR with whichever approach is preferred.

I've submitted a fix in #145659.

The root cause is that `Py_ReprLeave(dd->default_factory)` was called unconditionally in `defdict_repr`, even when `Py_ReprEnter` returned > 0 (recursion detected). When `Py_ReprEnter` detects recursion, it does not add a new entry to the tracking list - it just reports that the object is already being repr'd. Calling `Py_ReprLeave` in that case removes the entry from the outer call, so subsequent recursive calls bypass the guard entirely.

The fix moves `Py_ReprLeave` inside the `else` branch so it's only called when `Py_ReprEnter` returned 0 (successfully entered).

The ssl context issue is only an example of where this GC collection threshold change causes the problem.  Any time you have reference cycles that hold on to a significant amount of memory without having a large number of container objects, you will see the same issue.  I.e. sporadic higher memory usage.

Summarizing [Sergey's` tests](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/142001#issuecomment-3679312250), Python <= 3.14.1 will break cycles after about 1000 new container objects.  Versions >= 3.14.2 will break cycles after about 4600 new container objects.  However, it's not very predicable about how many new container objects it takes before it actually looks for cycles.

If your program doesn't create cycles or those cycles don't consume a lot of memory relative to the number of container objects in them, the 3.14.2 change doesn't hurt.  It even gives a performance boost, since the GC runs less often.
